Antimicrobial Groups & Antimicrobial Resistance 1 & 2 PHARMACOLOGY — TRANS 2.08 V2 · Dr. Faye Karissa Lourdes M. Bautista, MD, FPCP, FPCCP

Overview of the Whole Lecture

A single-page orientation to the entire trans. Use this tab to see the framework first, then open the lesson tabs that follow.

What this lecture is about

  • The lecture surveys the major antibacterial drug groups and organises them by mechanism of action rather than by disease.
  • Four mechanism families carry the whole lesson.
    • Cell wall and cell membrane agents — beta-lactams, glycopeptides, daptomycin and related drugs.
    • Protein synthesis inhibitors — agents acting on the 30S or the 50S ribosomal subunit.
    • Antimetabolites — folate pathway antagonists.
    • Nucleic acid synthesis inhibitors — fluoroquinolones, plus rifamycins in the comprehensive review.
  • Every group is then examined through the same four recurring questions used by the lecturer.
    • What is the target?
    • Why is the target selectively toxic to bacteria?
    • How does resistance occur?
    • What toxicities limit clinical use?
  • The last third of the lecture shifts from drugs to safe prescribing — adverse effects, special populations, drug interactions, resistance and stewardship.

Learning objectives stated in the lecture page 1

  • Define antimicrobial drugs and antibiotics.
  • Define bacteriostatic antimicrobial drugs.
  • Define bactericidal antimicrobial drugs.
  • Differentiate between bacteriostatic and bactericidal drugs.
  • Classify antibiotics according to the spectrum of activity.
  • Classify antibiotics according to the mechanism of action.
  • Discuss the individual mechanisms of action of the major antibiotic groups — beta-lactams, protein synthesis inhibitors, nucleic acid synthesis inhibitors and folate antagonists.

The Master Framework — Target Map

BACTERIAL TARGET
  • Cell wall synthesis
    • Penicillins · Cephalosporins · Carbapenems · Monobactams · Vancomycin → usually bactericidal
  • Cell membrane
    • Daptomycin · Polymyxins → bactericidal
  • 30S ribosome
    • Aminoglycosides (cidal) · Tetracyclines (static)
  • 50S ribosome
    • Macrolides · Clindamycin · Chloramphenicol · Linezolid · Streptogramins → mostly static, may be cidal for selected organisms
  • Folate synthesis
    • Sulfonamides + Trimethoprim → sequential combination is often bactericidal
  • DNA replication
    • Fluoroquinolones → bactericidal
  • RNA synthesis
    • Rifamycins → bactericidal

Structure adapted from Table 12, Antibacterials at a glance, page 22.

Must Know — Memory Map CELL WALL = beta-lactams and vancomycin.
30S = aminoglycosides and tetracyclines.
50S = macrolides, clindamycin, chloramphenicol and linezolid.
FOLATE = sulfonamide plus trimethoprim.
DNA = fluoroquinolones.

Must-Know Concepts Before You Start

Key Differentiator — Cidal versus Static Bactericidal: causes irreversible bacterial death.
Often preferred in endocarditis, meningitis, severe infection or marked immunosuppression.
Bacteriostatic: reversibly inhibits growth and relies more on host clearance.
Not intrinsically weaker — efficacy depends on organism, site, exposure and host.
Clinical Cue — Selective Toxicity Selective toxicity means greater injury to the microorganism than to the host.
It is achieved by targeting the cell wall, the 70S ribosome, folate synthesis or bacterial enzymes that humans either lack or use differently.
Must Know — Two Mnemonics the Lecturer Gave Protein synthesis inhibitors: "Buy AT 30, CELL for 50".
AT = Aminoglycosides and Tetracyclines act on 30S.
CELL = Chloramphenicol, Erythromycin, Linezolid and Lincosamides act on 50S.
Beta-lactam escape: destroy the drug, change the target, keep the drug out, pump the drug out.

Tab Summary

What this lesson asks you to hold in mind

  • One organising question runs through every section — what bacterial structure does the drug attack, and why does the host survive it
    • Selective toxicity comes from the peptidoglycan wall, the 70S ribosome and the folate synthesis pathway.
    • Human cells have no wall, an 80S ribosome and absorb preformed folate.
  • Five target families account for almost every agent named in the lecture
    • Cell wall and membrane — beta-lactams, glycopeptides, daptomycin, polymyxins
    • 30S ribosome — aminoglycosides and tetracyclines
    • 50S ribosome — macrolides, clindamycin, chloramphenicol, linezolid
    • Folate — sulfonamides plus trimethoprim
    • Nucleic acid — fluoroquinolones and rifamycins
  • Cidal versus static is a tendency, not a verdict
    • The label shifts with organism, concentration, growth phase and site.
    • It matters most in endocarditis, meningitis and neutropenia.
  • Resistance is treated as a consequence of prescribing
    • That framing is why stewardship and the 48 to 72 hour timeout reappear in the later tabs.
  • How to use the remaining tabs
    • Tabs 2 to 17 follow the lecture in order.
    • Tabs 18 to 23 are the Comprehensive Reviewer, which restates every class in a fixed format.
    • The Comparison Sheet and Cram Sheet are the last two tabs.

I.A — Beta-Lactams: Penicillin

Origin and chemistry, the classification families, how PBP mimicry kills the cell, the four escape strategies, kinetics and toxicity.

Overview and Chemistry

Overview page 1

  • In 1941, penicillin was accidentally obtained from the fungus Penicillium notatum.
  • Currently it is largely obtained from Penicillium chrysogenum.
  • Penicillin is a cell wall synthesis inhibitor.
  • Used mainly against Gram-positive bacteria.

Chemistry page 1

  • The mainly used penicillin is Penicillin G, also called benzylpenicillin.
  • The antibacterial and bactericidal activity is due to the beta-lactam ring.
    • The beta-lactam ring is attached to a thiazolidine ring.
    • COOH plus sodium forms a salt to achieve greater stability.
    • Amidases substitute the amide group to produce semisynthetic penicillins.
  • Base architecture — the 6-aminopenicillanic acid nucleus, an A-ring thiazolidine fused to a B-ring beta-lactam.
Figure 1. 6-Aminopenicillanic Acid with beta-lactam ring (B) and Thiazolidine Ring (A). Katzung 16th Ed, Fig 43-1 · page 1
What to notice: the two fused rings are labelled A and B. Ring B is the four-membered beta-lactam that carries the bactericidal activity, and ring A is the thiazolidine. The R group on the left is the side chain that amidases replace to create the semisynthetic penicillins.

Classification

Even though there are different kinds of penicillins, all of them interfere with bacterial cell wall synthesis. Modification of the side chain is what changes the properties of each agent.

Table 1. Properties of beta-lactams and examples page 1
ClassificationExamples
Acid-resistantPenicillin V
Penicillinase-resistantMethicillin, Cloxacillin
Extended-spectrumAmoxicillin, Ampicillin, Carbenicillin, Piperacillin
Beta-lactamase inhibitorsClavulanic acid, Sulbactam, Tazobactam

Mechanism of Action

1Inhibits transpeptidases, the enzymes responsible for the stability and rigidity of the bacterial cell wall.
▼
2Inhibits the suppression of autolysis, which means autolysis is actively promoted.
▼
3Produces a cell wall-deficient (CWD) bacterium.
▼
4The cell becomes hyperosmotic.
▼
5The cell swells → bursts → dies.

Molecular Mimicry of Beta-Lactams — 01, Molecular Deception

Recognition of PBPs and the terminal D-Ala-D-Ala substrate page 2

  • During normal peptidoglycan synthesis, penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) recognise the terminal D-Ala-D-Ala portion of the peptide precursor.
    • Beta-lactam antibiotics structurally resemble this substrate.
    • Because of this molecular mimicry, the PBP recognises the beta-lactam and binds to it.
    • Instead of completing normal transpeptidation, the beta-lactam forms a stable covalent complex with the enzyme.
    • The PBP is therefore functionally inactivated.
  • Failure of peptidoglycan cross-linking follows, which progressively weakens the bacterial cell wall.
  • Beta-lactams work best against actively dividing bacteria, because those organisms are actively synthesising their cell wall.
Figure 2. Molecular Deception — Binding Mechanism. Lecturer's PPT · page 2
What to notice: the figure pairs the natural D-Ala-D-Ala substrate on the left with the beta-lactam antibiotic on the right and shows that the beta-lactam ring mimics the stereochemical structure of D-Ala-D-Ala, tricking the enzyme. The lower panel shows irreversible covalent inhibition, where the PBP binds the drug and forms a stable inactive complex that halts wall construction.

Molecular Mimicry of Beta-Lactams — 02, Lethal Cascade

Cellular collapse page 2

  • Beta-lactams disturb the normal balance between cell wall synthesis and cell wall degradation.
    • Bacterial autolytic enzymes, or autolysins, continue to break down existing peptidoglycan.
    • Because no peptidoglycan can be properly cross-linked, the bacterium progressively loses the structural integrity of its wall.
  • Why this is bactericidal
    • Bacteria live under considerable internal osmotic pressure.
    • Once the wall is sufficiently weak it can no longer withstand the pressure.
    • Water enters, the bacterium swells, and the cell undergoes osmotic lysis.
Wall synthesis blocked→ Autolysins keep degrading→ Structural integrity lost→ Water influx and osmotic lysis
Figure 3. Lethal Cascade — Cellular Collapse. Lecturer's PPT · page 2
What to notice: the three labelled stages run top to bottom — autolysin (murein hydrolase) activation, then loss of osmotic integrity as the weakened wall can no longer resist high internal pressure, then bactericidal osmotic lysis as rapid water influx ruptures the cell during active growth.

Penicillin Families and Their Targets

Table 2. Classification of beta-lactams with examples and characteristics page 1
ClassificationDrugs, innovation and targets
Natural penicillins Drugs: Penicillin G (IV), Penicillin V (oral, acid-stable).
Lecture memory cue: PEN V — Vunganga, meaning mouth, so Penicillin V is the oral one.
Targets: Gram-positive cocci, Gram-negative cocci such as meningococci, and spirochetes such as syphilis.
Vulnerability: highly susceptible to beta-lactamase hydrolysis.
Antistaphylococcal penicillins Drugs: Nafcillin (IV), Oxacillin (IV), Dicloxacillin (oral).
Innovation — steric shields: bulky side chains protect the beta-lactam ring from staphylococcal penicillinases.
Targets: narrow spectrum, MSSA.
Warning: inactive against MRSA.
Extended-spectrum Aminopenicillins: Ampicillin (IV or oral) and Amoxicillin (oral, high bioavailability).
Antipseudomonal: Piperacillin (IV).
Targets: improved Gram-negative rod coverage. Piperacillin targets Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Clinical note: often paired with beta-lactamase inhibitors to restore activity — clavulanic acid, tazobactam, sulbactam.

Structural Modification Across the Beta-Lactams

  • All of these agents contain a beta-lactam ring.
  • Structural modifications influence four things.
    • Antimicrobial spectrum
    • Resistance to beta-lactamases
    • Pharmacokinetics
    • Route of administration
Figure 5. Structural Modifications in Beta-Lactams. Lecturer's PPT · page 3
What to notice: the beta-lactam ring is highlighted in every one of the four structures — penicillin, cephalosporin, monobactam and carbapenem. What differs is the ring fused to it, and in the monobactam there is no fused ring at all. This single visual explains why the whole family shares one mechanism but differs in spectrum and in beta-lactamase stability.
Table 4. Structural modifications in beta-lactams — side chain drives spectrum and route page 3
Drug nameSpectrum of activityRoute
Penicillin GGram-positive and a few Gram-negativeParenteral
Penicillin VSimilar to penicillin GOral
AmpicillinGram-positive and more Gram-negative than penicillinParenteral and oral
AmoxicillinSimilar to ampicillinOral, better absorbed than ampicillin
MethicillinGram-positive only, including beta-lactamase producersParenteral

Indications and Side Effects

Indications page 1

  • Pharyngitis and laryngitis
  • Rheumatic fever
  • Pneumococcal infections
  • Gonorrhea and syphilis
  • Diphtheria and tetanus
  • Gas gangrene
  • Rat-bite fever
  • Anthrax
  • Prophylactic use: bacterial endocarditis and rheumatic fever

Side effects page 1

  • Local irritation and pain at the site of injection
  • Thrombophlebitis
  • Muscular twitching and convulsions
  • Bleeding due to interference with platelets
  • Hallucinations
  • Hypersensitivity reactions such as rashes, allergy and photosensitivity

Four Main Biochemical Strategies to Evade Beta-Lactams

Table 3. Bacterial strategies to avoid beta-lactams page 2
StrategyDescription
Enzymatic inactivation — beta-lactamases
Destroy the drug		 Production of beta-lactamases such as penicillinases, cephalosporinases and carbapenemases.
These hydrolyze the beta-lactam ring, converting it into inactive penicilloic acid.
Target site PBP modification
Change the target		 Synthesis of PBPs with low binding affinity for beta-lactams.
Best example — PBP2a in MRSA, encoded by mecA, and altered PBPs in resistant S. pneumoniae.
Impaired drug penetration in Gram-negatives
Keep the drug out		 Loss or mutation of outer membrane channel proteins, the porins.
This blocks hydrophilic beta-lactams from crossing the outer membrane of Gram-negative pathogens.
Active transmembrane efflux
Pump the drug out		 Active multidrug efflux pumps physically pump beta-lactams out of the periplasmic space of Gram-negative bacteria, preventing a toxic concentration from building up.
Must Know — Mechanisms to Evade Beta-Lactams Destroy the drug.
Change the target.
Keep the drug out.
Pump the drug out.

Penicillin Kinetics

Clearance, interactions and penetration page 2

  • Active renal clearance
    • Excreted rapidly by the kidneys — 10 percent glomerular filtration and 90 percent active tubular secretion.
    • Half-life is brief, normally less than 1 hour.
  • Probenecid interaction
    • Probenecid competitively blocks active tubular secretion, raising serum concentrations and prolonging the penicillin half-life.
  • Biliary clearance exception
    • Nafcillin is cleared primarily by biliary excretion and needs no dose adjustment in renal impairment.
    • Oxacillin uses both renal and biliary routes.
  • Tissue penetration
    • Excellent levels in pleural, pericardial, peritoneal and synovial fluids.
    • Ceftriaxone and cefotaxime cross the blood-brain barrier to reach therapeutic levels in inflamed CSF.
  • Renal clearance of the wider group
    • Most are excreted renally by glomerular filtration and tubular secretion.
    • Ceftriaxone is the exception — eliminated primarily by biliary excretion, so no renal dose adjustment is required.

Toxicities and Adverse Effects

Must Know — Hypersensitivity is the Major Adverse Effect Reactions range from mild maculopapular rashes to severe, life-threatening anaphylactic shock, seen in about 0.05 percent of patients.
Breakdown products such as penicillinic acid bound to host proteins act as hapten antigens.

Other toxicities page 2

  • Neurotoxicity and seizures
    • Extremely high doses can provoke severe seizures, confusion or encephalopathy, particularly in patients with pre-existing renal dysfunction because of drug accumulation.
  • Organ-specific damage
    • Nafcillin can cause neutropenia.
    • Oxacillin is associated with hepatitis.
    • Methicillin causes acute interstitial nephritis, and its clinical use is now obsolete.
Clinical Cue — If You See X, Think Y Penicillin plus neutropenia → think nafcillin.
Penicillin plus hepatitis → think oxacillin.
Penicillin plus acute interstitial nephritis → think methicillin.
Penicillin with no renal dose adjustment → think nafcillin and its biliary clearance.

Tab Summary

Penicillins in five moves

  • Mechanism
    • The beta-lactam ring mimics D-Ala-D-Ala and acylates the transpeptidase PBP.
    • Cross-linking fails, autolysins finish the wall, and the cell lyses osmotically.
    • Killing requires actively dividing bacteria and is time-dependent.
  • Four families, four one-line identities
    • Natural — streptococci and syphilis, and penicillin G is acid-labile.
    • Anti-staphylococcal — MSSA only, never MRSA.
    • Aminopenicillins — add enterococci, and rash with EBV.
    • Antipseudomonal — piperacillin, usually paired with tazobactam.
  • Four ways bacteria escape
    • Beta-lactamase production
    • Altered PBPs
    • Reduced porin entry
    • Efflux
  • Kinetics worth remembering
    • Renal elimination, with probenecid blocking tubular secretion.
    • Oral options are penicillin V and amoxicillin.
  • Toxicity
    • Hypersensitivity, with anaphylaxis at about 0.05 percent.
    • Interstitial nephritis, cytopenias and C. difficile diarrhea.
    • Seizures at high serum levels, especially in renal failure.

I.B — Beta-Lactams: Cephalosporins

Same wall target as penicillin but different binding proteins, five generations with a clear spectrum trend, and three class-specific toxicities.

Overview and Chemistry

Overview page 2

  • Semi-synthetic and bactericidal.
  • Derived from Acremonium chrysogenum, formerly known as Cephalosporium acremonium, a fungus.
  • Cell wall synthesis inhibitor acting by interacting with PBPs.
  • Spectrum is entirely different from penicillin.
  • Among the most commonly prescribed antibiotics.
  • Have several generations depending on their spectrum.

Chemistry page 2

  • Have a beta-lactam ring combined with a dihydrothiazine ring, in contrast to the thiazolidine ring of penicillin.
  • At position 7 of the beta-lactam ring, amidases allow further substitution to achieve differences in
    • Potency
    • Efficacy
    • Pharmacokinetic parameters
Figure 4. Penicillin versus Cephalosporin structure, with a dihydrothiazine ring instead of a thiazolidine ring (A). Katzung 16th Ed, Fig 43-2 · page 3
What to notice: both nuclei keep the same four-membered beta-lactam ring (B). The difference is ring A — a five-membered thiazolidine in penicillin against a six-membered dihydrothiazine in cephalosporin. The cephalosporin nucleus is therefore called substituted 7-aminocephalosporanic acid, and the extra R2 position gives an additional site for modification.

Mechanism of Action and Resistance

Mechanism of action page 3

The mechanism is similar to penicillin, but the binding proteins are different.

  • Inhibit transpeptidases.
  • Promote autolysis.
  • Increase cell wall deficiency (CWD).

Mechanism of resistance page 3

  • Change in affinity of transpeptidases.
  • Change in structure of transpeptidases.
  • Production of penicillinase (beta-lactamase).
  • Decreased permeability of the cell wall.

Cephalosporin Evolution Across Generations

Key Differentiator — The Generational Trend From early to later generations, Gram-negative coverage tends to increase.
The trend is useful but incomplete, because the exceptions are what get tested — Pseudomonas activity and MRSA activity do not follow a simple line.
Table 5. Cephalosporin generations, characteristics and agents page 3
GenerationDrugs, focus and landmark use
1st Generation Drugs: Cefazolin (IV), Cephalexin (oral).
Focus: Gram-positive. Minimal Gram-negative coverage. Inactive against MRSA.
Landmark: gold standard for surgical perioperative prophylaxis and skin infections.
2nd Generation Drugs: Cefuroxime, Cefoxitin, Cefotetan.
Focus: expanded Gram-negative coverage including H. influenzae. Cefoxitin and cefotetan are active against anaerobes such as B. fragilis.
Landmark: surgical prophylaxis in abdominal and pelvic procedures, upper respiratory infections.
3rd Generation Drugs: Ceftriaxone, Cefotaxime, Ceftazidime.
Focus: massive Gram-negative coverage. Penetrates the blood-brain barrier. Ceftazidime is active against Pseudomonas.
Landmark: empirical meningitis therapy, community-acquired pneumonia and gonorrhea with ceftriaxone.
4th Generation Drug: Cefepime (IV).
Focus: ultra-broad spectrum, highly active against Gram-positives, Gram-negatives and Pseudomonas. Resistant to AmpC beta-lactamases.
Landmark: empirical nosocomial infections and febrile neutropenia.
5th Generation Drug: Ceftaroline fosamil (IV).
Focus: anti-MRSA and uniquely active against MRSA through high binding affinity to altered PBP2a. Broad Gram-negative coverage similar to 3rd generation.
Landmark: complicated skin and soft tissue infections, community-acquired pneumonia.

Generation summary as stated in the lecture page 3

  • First generation — Cefazolin, Cephalexin.
    • Strong Gram-positive activity. Important for surgical prophylaxis.
  • Second generation — Cefoxitin, Cefuroxime, Cefaclor.
    • Expanded Gram-negative coverage plus anaerobic activity.
  • Third generation — Ceftriaxone, Cefotaxime, Ceftazidime.
    • Substantially greater Gram-negative activity.
    • Ceftriaxone and cefotaxime are important in meningitis.
    • Ceftazidime provides Pseudomonas coverage.
  • Fourth generation — Cefepime.
    • Broad Gram-positive and Gram-negative activity.
    • Uses — severe hospital-acquired infections, febrile neutropenia, infections caused by P. aeruginosa.
  • Fifth generation — Ceftaroline.
    • Broad spectrum and active against MRSA.
    • Uses — skin and soft tissue infections, complicated cases, community-acquired pneumonia, MRSA infections.
Must Know — Cephalosporin Generation Memory Aid from the Lecture 1st generation — FA or PH: ceFAzolin, ceFAdroxil, cePHAlexin, cePHAlotin. Except cefaclor.
3rd generation — ONE, TEN or IME: ceftriaxONE, ceftibuTEN, cefotaxIME, ceftazidIME, cefpodoxIME. Except cefuroxime.
4th generation — PI: cefePIme, cefPIrome.
5th generation — ROL: ceftaROLine, ceftobupROLe.
2nd generation — everything else: cefoxitin, cefotetan, cefmetazole, cefprozil, cefackir, cefuroxime, cefaclor.
Figure 6. Cephalosporin Summary. Lecturer's PPT · page 29
What to notice: the left grid tracks the spectrum shift generation by generation — G positive at the top, progressively more G negative going down, with the exceptions flagged in each row such as not active against Pseudomonas for 1st, 2nd and ceftriaxone, and added MRSA coverage only at the 5th. The right panel repeats the four evasion mechanisms under Resistance — beta-lactamases including ESBL and AmpC, altered PBPs, decreased permeability from porin loss, and efflux pumps. The exam tip at the bottom pairs each generation with its landmark indication.

Indications and Side Effects

Indications page 3

  • Alternative to penicillin
  • Upper respiratory tract infections
  • Urinary and soft tissue infections
  • Septicemia
  • Pharyngitis and meningitis
  • Gonorrhea and typhoid fever
  • Mixed aerobic and anaerobic infections
  • Hospital-acquired infections
  • Surgical prophylaxis

Side effects page 3

  • Pain at the injection site and thrombophlebitis
  • Diarrhea
  • Hypersensitivity reactions such as rashes, shock and photosensitivity
  • Cross-reactions in patients with penicillin allergy
  • Hemolysis
  • Nephrotoxicity
  • Hematologic adverse effects

Class-Specific Toxicity and Adverse Effects

Must Know — Cross Allergy Cross-allergenicity with penicillins is approximately 5 to 10 percent.
Cephalosporins are contraindicated in patients with a history of severe immediate penicillin hypersensitivity, meaning anaphylaxis.

Specific tissue class toxicity page 3

  • Neonatal jaundice
    • Ceftriaxone can displace bilirubin from serum albumin, posing a serious risk of kernicterus in neonates. It should be avoided in newborns.
  • Biliary pseudolithiasis
    • Ceftriaxone has a high affinity for biliary calcium, occasionally leading to calcium-ceftriaxone precipitation in the gallbladder.
  • Methylthiotetrazole (MTT) ring
    • Cefotetan and cefamandole contain an MTT side chain.
    • This inhibits vitamin K synthesis, causing hypoprothrombinemia and bleeding risk.
    • It also provokes a severe disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.
Do Not Confuse — Ceftriaxone Has Two Separate Biliary Problems Bilirubin displacement: ceftriaxone pushes bilirubin off albumin → free bilirubin crosses into the neonatal brain → kernicterus.
Calcium precipitation: ceftriaxone binds biliary calcium → sludge in the gallbladder → biliary pseudolithiasis.
Both are ceftriaxone, but one is a neonatal neurologic risk and the other is a gallbladder problem.

Tab Summary

Cephalosporins in three moves

  • Same mechanism, different scaffold
    • Beta-lactams that bind PBPs and are bactericidal and time-dependent.
    • The dihydrothiazine ring allows more side-chain modification than the penicillin nucleus.
  • The generational trend and the exceptions that beat it
    • Moving up the generations adds Gram-negative reach and initially costs Gram-positive reach.
    • Ceftazidime and cefepime cover Pseudomonas.
    • Ceftaroline covers MRSA.
    • Ceftriaxone and cefotaxime enter the CSF.
    • Cephamycins add anaerobes.
  • Safety points that get tested
    • 5 to 10 percent cross-allergy with penicillins.
    • Cefepime neurotoxicity in renal dysfunction.
    • Ceftriaxone biliary sludging and the neonatal calcium interaction.
    • MTT side-chain agents causing hypoprothrombinemia and a disulfiram-like reaction.

I.C and I.D — Monobactams, Beta-Lactamase Inhibitors and Carbapenems

The narrowest beta-lactam and the broadest beta-lactam, plus the suicide inhibitors that rescue partner drugs.

C. Monobactams

Overview page 4

  • Monocyclic, naturally occurring antibiotics isolated from Chromobacterium species.
  • The beta-lactam ring is not fused to another ring, in contrast to most other beta-lactams.
  • Effective only against aerobic Gram-negative bacteria, for example Neisseria and Pseudomonas.

Chemistry

  • The four-membered ring at the bottom is the beta-lactam ring.
  • There is a second thiazole ring, but it is not fused to the beta-lactam ring.

Drugs and mechanisms page 4

Drugs

  • Aztreonam
  • Tigemonam
  • Carumonam
  • Nocardicin

Mechanism of action

  • Work only against aerobic Gram-negative bacteria.
  • Inhibit synthesis of the peptidoglycan layer by binding to and inhibiting PBPs, which are the transpeptidases.

Mechanism of resistance

  • Change in affinity of transpeptidases.
  • Change in structure of transpeptidases.
  • Most bacteria produce or form beta-lactamases.

Uses page 4

  • Hospital-acquired infections originating from the urinary, biliary, gastrointestinal and female genital tracts
  • Cystic fibrosis
  • Skin infections
  • Pyelonephritis, a severe kidney infection
  • Septicemia
  • Peritonitis
  • Endometritis

Side effects page 4

  • Skin rash
  • Occasional abnormal liver function
  • Cross-sensitivity with cephalosporin allergy
  • Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and abdominal pain
  • Abnormal taste in the mouth

Aztreonam — the monobactam for Gram-negative aerobes

  • Narrower spectrum of activity
    • Binds PBPs and inhibits peptidoglycan activity.
    • Active against Gram-negative aerobes only, combined with a favourable allergy profile.
    • Useful when Gram-negative coverage is needed with zero beta-lactam allergy risk.
    • Not useful against Gram-positive bacteria.
  • Monocyclic core
    • A unique monocyclic beta-lactam ring that stands alone, unfused to another ring structure.
    • This prevents recognition by antibodies, hence no cross allergy.
    • However, a patient allergic to ceftazidime will also react to aztreonam because they share an identical chemical side chain.
  • Aerobic Gram-negative focus
    • Selectively active against aerobic Gram-negative rods, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
    • Lacks Gram-positive and anaerobic coverage.
  • No cross-allergenicity
    • Generally safe for severe penicillin-allergic patients who have a Gram-negative infection.
Exam Trap — The One Aztreonam Allergy Exception Aztreonam is the safe beta-lactam in severe penicillin allergy.
The single exception is ceftazidime, because the two drugs carry an identical side chain.

Beta-Lactamase Inhibitors

Suicide inhibitors page 4

  • What they are
    • Molecules — clavulanic acid, sulbactam and tazobactam — structurally related to beta-lactams but possessing weak inherent antibacterial activity.
  • Mechanism
    • Covalently bind and irreversibly inactivate serine beta-lactamases, especially Class A plasmid-mediated enzymes, protecting the co-administered antibiotic.
  • Clinical synergies
    • Amoxicillin-clavulanate — oral, Augmentin.
    • Ampicillin-sulbactam — IV, Unasyn.
    • Piperacillin-tazobactam — IV, Zosyn.

D. Carbapenems

Overview page 4

  • Among the broadest-spectrum beta-lactam antibiotics. The lecture calls them the big guns.
  • Important agents: Imipenem, Meropenem, Doripenem, Ertapenem.
  • Inhibit cell wall synthesis through PBPs, and their strong beta-lactamase inhibition gives excellent stability against many beta-lactamases.
  • Very broad spectrum, so they are generally reserved for serious infections, particularly those involving resistant organisms.
  • Thienamycin was the first carbapenem discovered, in 1976.
  • Extremely potent bactericidal and broad-spectrum beta-lactam antibiotics.

Chemistry

  • Very similar to the penicillins, also called penams.
  • The sulfur atom at position 1 has been replaced with a carbon atom.
  • Unsaturation has been introduced, which gives the group its name — carbapenems.
Must Know — Stewardship Message Carbapenems should be used judiciously.
The emergence of carbapenem resistance significantly limits treatment options.
Table 6. Classification of carbapenems page 4
ClassificationExamples
Group 1Ertapenem
Group 2Imipenem, Meropenem, Doripenem

Mechanism of action page 4

  • Resistant to most beta-lactamases and inhibit penicillinase-producing staphylococci and some MRSA.
  • Penetrate the bacterial cell wall and bind to protein-binding target sites.
  • Interfere with synthesis of vital cell wall components, which leads to cell death.

Mechanism of resistance page 4

  • Decreased permeability of the cell wall.
  • Modification of target sites through genetic mutations.
  • Modifications in beta-lactamase enzymes.

Uses page 4

  • Nosocomial infections such as septicemia, febrile neutropenia, intra-abdominal and pelvic infections
  • Respiratory tract infections
  • ENT infections
  • Genitourinary infections
  • Multidrug-resistant infections

Side effects page 4

  • Seizures at higher doses
  • Diarrhea and vomiting
  • Skin rashes
  • Cross-sensitivity in patients with penicillin allergy
  • Headache, loss of appetite, tiredness and pruritus

Class profile and clinical warnings

  • Ultra-broad spectrum
    • Doripenem, ertapenem, imipenem and meropenem possess a carbapenem nucleus conferring exceptional stability against most bacterial beta-lactamases.
  • Imipenem and cilastatin
    • Imipenem is cleaved by renal dehydropeptidase-1 in the proximal tubules, leading to low urinary levels and toxic metabolites, so it is co-administered with cilastatin, an inhibitor of that enzyme.
  • Other carbapenems
    • Meropenem and doripenem are stable to dehydropeptidase-1 and do not require cilastatin.
    • Ertapenem is long-acting but lacks activity against Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter.
  • Seizure risk
    • Imipenem lowers the seizure threshold.
    • Seizures are most common in patients with renal failure or pre-existing CNS lesions receiving high-dose regimens.
  • Renal adjustment
    • All carbapenems are cleared renally and require careful dose reduction in renal insufficiency to prevent systemic accumulation and CNS toxicity.
  • Cross-allergies
    • Partial cross-reactivity exists with penicillins.
    • Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and localised infusion site irritation are common.
Table 7. Important distinctions between carbapenem agents page 5
DrugInformation
Imipenem Hydrolyzed by dihydropeptidase-1.
This enzyme sits in the brush border of the proximal tubules, inactivates imipenem and generates nephrotoxic metabolites.
To prevent this, imipenem is co-administered with cilastatin, which blocks dihydropeptidase-1.
Meropenem, Doripenem and Ertapenem Do not need cilastatin.
They are structurally modified to resist dihydropeptidase-1.
Ertapenem Unique because it lacks activity against Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter.
This limits its use in nosocomial infections and in highly resistant Gram-negative infections.
Must Know — Toxicity of Imipenem Imipenem is notorious for causing seizures.
Risk is increased at high doses and in patients with renal failure.
Mechanism: it competes with GABA binding at the receptor level and provokes neurotoxicity.
Action: if a patient develops a seizure, discontinue the drug.
Clinical Cue — If You See X, Think Y Carbapenem plus cilastatin → imipenem only.
Carbapenem that is once daily but not antipseudomonal → ertapenem.
Beta-lactam in a severe penicillin allergy needing Gram-negative cover → aztreonam, unless the allergy is to ceftazidime.

Tab Summary

Monobactams, inhibitors and carbapenems

  • Aztreonam
    • A monobactam hitting aerobic Gram-negative PBPs, including Pseudomonas.
    • No Gram-positive and no anaerobic activity.
    • Usable in severe beta-lactam allergy, except for the shared ceftazidime side chain.
  • Beta-lactamase inhibitors
    • Clavulanate, sulbactam and tazobactam are suicide inhibitors of class A enzymes.
    • Avibactam and relebactam are non-beta-lactam inhibitors reaching class A, C and some D.
    • Vaborbactam plus meropenem is aimed at KPC.
    • None of them help against altered PBP, permeability or efflux.
  • Carbapenems
    • Derived from thienamycin, discovered in 1976.
    • Bind multiple PBPs and resist most beta-lactamases, giving the broadest spectrum in the lecture.
    • Imipenem needs cilastatin and carries the greatest seizure risk through GABA inhibition.
    • Meropenem is the CNS agent.
    • Ertapenem is once daily and not antipseudomonal.
  • Stewardship framing
    • Carbapenems are explicitly reserved so that activity is preserved.

II — Glycopeptides: Vancomycin, Oritavancin and Teicoplanin

A different way to stop wall synthesis — bind the substrate instead of the enzyme.

A. Vancomycin

Overview page 5

  • Brand names: First-Vancomycin 25, First-Vancomycin 50, Firvanq, Vancocin.
  • Drug class: glycopeptide antibiotic.
  • Dosing route: oral, continuous infusion or intermittent injection.
  • Coverage: Gram-positive bacteria.
  • Route of elimination: through the kidneys, excreted in urine by glomerular filtration.
  • Half-life: 6 hours.

Indications page 5

  • Septicemia
  • Infective endocarditis
  • Bone infections
  • Skin and skin structure infections
  • Pneumonia
  • MRSA infections
  • Clostridium difficile infections
    • Patients may have watery or bloody diarrhea with inflammation of the colon and small intestine.
    • Oral vancomycin is not significantly absorbed into the bloodstream and therefore acts mainly within the intestines.

Mechanism of action — bind the substrate, not the enzyme

  • Vancomycin is a massive, water-soluble tricyclic glycopeptide with a molecular weight around 1500, produced by Amycolatopsis orientalis.
  • Unlike beta-lactams, vancomycin does not inhibit PBPs. It interacts directly with the peptidoglycan precursor.
  • It forms hydrogen bonds with the D-alanyl-D-alanine moiety of the NAM and NAG peptides on the wall of Gram-positive organisms.
    • Five hydrogen bonds are formed with this dipeptide.
    • This caps the precursor and sterically blocks the next two steps.
  • Capping prevents both enzymes from working.
    • Transglycosylase can no longer link the sugars, meaning no glycan chain elongation.
    • Transpeptidase can no longer cross-link the peptides.
  • This happens outside the cell membrane and at a late stage of cell wall assembly.
  • Why Gram-positives only: vancomycin is a large molecule and cannot pass through the narrow outer membrane porin channels of Gram-negative bacteria.
Vancomycin binds D-Ala-D-Ala→ Precursor capped by 5 hydrogen bonds→ Transglycosylase and transpeptidase both blocked→ Cell wall construction halts
Key Differentiator — Beta-Lactam versus Vancomycin Beta-lactams target the PBP transpeptidase enzyme by mimicking the substrate.
Vancomycin targets the substrate itself, the terminal D-Ala-D-Ala of the nascent pentapeptide.
That single difference explains why vancomycin resistance works by changing the substrate rather than the enzyme.

Mechanism of resistance

  • Target alteration to D-Ala-D-Lac
    • VRE and VRSA substitute the terminal D-alanine for D-lactate, seen in the VanA and VanB phenotypes, or for D-serine.
    • Chemically this replaces an NH group with an oxygen atom.
  • Loss of a hydrogen bond
    • This single biochemical substitution removes one critical hydrogen bond.
    • Binding affinity falls approximately 1,000-fold, which renders the drug ineffective.
    • This is the genetic basis of vancomycin-resistant strains — VRE and VISA.
  • Thickened cell wall in VISA
    • Vancomycin-intermediate S. aureus synthesises thickened cell walls with excess non-functional D-Ala-D-Ala targets that sequester vancomycin and prevent it from reaching active membrane sites.

Pharmacokinetics and clinical use

  • Parenteral for systemic MRSA
    • Poor oral absorption, so it must be given intravenously for systemic infections such as endocarditis, bloodstream infections and bone or joint infections caused by MRSA.
  • Oral for C. difficile colitis
    • Oral administration is reserved exclusively for C. difficile colitis, because the drug is not absorbed and stays highly concentrated in the GI tract.
  • Renal clearance and therapeutic drug monitoring
    • 90 percent excreted by glomerular filtration.
    • Accumulates in renal failure.
    • TDM is mandatory, with trough levels of 15 to 20 mcg per mL targeted for severe MRSA infections.
  • Drug-drug interactions listed in the lecture
    • Acyclovir, cefepime, ciprofloxacin, clindamycin, furosemide, gentamicin, ibuprofen, meloxicam, sirolimus, sulfamethoxazole, tacrolimus, tobramycin, metformin, methotrexate, naproxen and piperacillin-tazobactam.

Adverse effects and prevention

General adverse effects page 5

  • Stomach pain, nausea and diarrhea
  • Rash
  • Frequent urination
  • Ototoxicity
  • Red man syndrome
  • Acute kidney injury
Must Know — Red Man Syndrome An outdated term for the vancomycin infusion reaction or vancomycin flushing syndrome.
It presents as infusion-related flushing and an erythematous rash of the face and upper torso.
It is caused by non-immunologic direct mast-cell histamine release, so it is not a true allergic reaction — it is rate dependent.
Prevention: slow infusion over 1 to 2 hours or pre-treatment with antihistamines.

Organ toxicities in detail page 5

  • Nephrotoxicity
    • Dose-related acute kidney injury, described as very common.
    • Risk is significantly elevated with prolonged high trough levels, pre-existing renal dysfunction, or concurrent nephrotoxic drugs such as aminoglycosides.
    • Modern preparations are purer.
  • Ototoxicity
    • Less common and often irreversible.
    • Presents as tinnitus, vertigo or hearing loss.
    • Higher risk in patients with severe renal impairment.
Value Box — Trough Management for Vancomycin Target trough for severe infections: 15 to 20 mcg per mL.
If the trough is below target: administer vancomycin again.
If the trough is too high: skip the dose, then give the next scheduled dose.
To prevent red man syndrome: infuse slowly over 1 to 2 hours or give antihistamines beforehand.

B. Oritavancin

  • Mechanism: prevents transglycosylation and transpeptidation during cell wall synthesis by interfering with the processes involved in both steps.
  • Spectrum: activity focuses on Gram-positive organisms including resistant organisms.
  • Why it was developed: newer glycopeptides such as oritavancin retain strong Gram-positive activity while offering pharmacokinetic advantages over traditional agents.
  • Effective against VRS and VRE.
  • In phase IV trials for skin, soft tissue and MRSA infections.

C. Teicoplanin

Mechanism and concept page 6

  • A glycopeptide antibiotic with a mechanism similar to vancomycin.
    • Also binds the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursors and prevents proper cell wall synthesis.
    • Prevents cross-linking, which leads to cell lysis and death.
    • Bactericidal against Gram-positive organisms.
  • Concept cue from the lecture: think of teicoplanin as a vancomycin-type glycopeptide with prolonged pharmacokinetics and Gram-positive activity.

Spectrum of activity

  • Gram-positive bacteria, including
    • Staphylococcus aureus, including MRSA
    • Staphylococcus epidermidis
    • Streptococcus species
    • Enterococcus species
    • Clostridium difficile, as an alternative to vancomycin
  • Not active against Gram-negative organisms.

Pharmacokinetics

  • Long half-life of about 70 to 100 hours, allowing dosing every 3 to 4 days.
  • Excreted mostly unchanged.
  • Hot tissue penetration.

Clinical indications

  • MRSA and MRSE
  • Endocarditis
  • Bone and joint infections
  • Bacteremia and pneumonia
  • Skin and soft tissue infections
  • Infections in beta-lactam-allergic patients
  • C. difficile colitis using the oral form

Adverse effects

  • Rash and pruritus
  • Fever
  • Nephrotoxicity
  • Ototoxicity, rare
High-Yield Recap — Glycopeptides in One Look Shared mechanism: bind D-Ala-D-Ala and block transglycosylation plus transpeptidation.
Shared limit: Gram-positive only, because the molecule is too large for Gram-negative porins.
Shared toxicity theme: nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.
Vancomycin distinction: requires TDM and carries the infusion-rate reaction.
Teicoplanin distinction: very long half-life allows dosing every 3 to 4 days.
Oritavancin distinction: retains activity against VRS and VRE.

Tab Summary

Glycopeptides at a glance

  • Vancomycin mechanism
    • Binds the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus with 5 hydrogen bonds.
    • Blocks transglycosylation and transpeptidation by hiding the substrate, not the enzyme.
    • Gram-positive only, because the molecule cannot cross the Gram-negative outer membrane.
  • Resistance
    • D-Ala-D-Lac substitution in VRE causes a 1000-fold affinity loss.
    • Cell-wall thickening produces VISA.
  • Monitoring numbers
    • Target trough 15 to 20 mcg per mL in serious infection.
    • Trough drawn every 4th dose.
    • Half-life about 6 hours, with renal clearance.
  • Adverse effects
    • Red man syndrome is an infusion-rate reaction, not an allergy, and slow infusion prevents it.
    • Nephrotoxicity, neutropenia and rare ototoxicity.
  • Relatives
    • Teicoplanin has a 70 to 100 hour half-life.
    • Oritavancin is the long-acting single-dose option.
  • Two lines never to lose
    • Oral vancomycin treats only the gut lumen.
    • A beta-lactam beats vancomycin for MSSA.

II.D — Miscellaneous Cell Wall and Membrane Agents, plus Kinetic Red Flags

Daptomycin, bacitracin, fosfomycin and cycloserine, followed by the organ toxicity map and the clearance exceptions the lecturer emphasised.

01 — Daptomycin

  • Class: lipopeptide antibacterial.
  • Mechanism of action: binds to the bacterial plasma membrane, causing membrane depolarization and release of intracellular ions, leading to
    • Disruption of essential cellular processes
    • Cell damage and bacterial death
  • Contrast with vancomycin: vancomycin targets the cell wall precursor, whereas daptomycin disrupts membrane function.
  • Spectrum of activity: potent bactericidal activity against Gram-positive bacteria, including vancomycin-resistant strains of enterococci and S. aureus.
  • Adverse effects: GI disturbances, rash, headache and rarely muscle discomfort or weakness.
    • The important toxicity is muscle injury or myopathy. Muscle symptoms and creatine phosphatase may need to be monitored during therapy.
  • Indications: MRSA and vancomycin-resistant skin and soft tissue infections.

02 — Bacitracin

  • Mechanism: inhibitor of bacterial cell wall synthesis with activity against Gram-positive organisms.
  • Spectrum of activity: effective against Gram-positive organisms such as streptococci, staphylococci and enterococci.
    • Corynebacterium, gonococci, meningococci, Cl. tetani, Treponema and H. influenzae are highly sensitive.
  • Indications: topical antibiotic used as an antiseptic.
    • The lecture uses it as an example of how a drug may have good antibacterial activity but limited systemic application because of toxicity.
  • Resistance: organisms do not develop resistance.
  • Adverse effects: marked nephrotoxicity, which is why its use is limited to the topical form for skin and soft tissue infections.

03 — Fosfomycin

  • Class: phosphonic acid derivative.
  • Mechanism of action: inhibits an early step in peptidoglycan synthesis.
    • This distinguishes it from beta-lactams, which act later during cross-linking.
    • Bactericidal.
  • Spectrum of activity: S. aureus, streptococci, Enterobacteriaceae, H. influenzae and Neisseria are susceptible.
  • Synergy: synergistic effect with penicillins, cephalosporins and aminoglycosides.
  • Indications: oral fosfomycin is used for UTI.
    • A 3 g oral dose is used to treat UTIs in women.
    • Because it acts through a distinct mechanism, it can remain useful against organisms resistant to other antimicrobial classes.
  • Adverse effects: GI distress, skin rash, exacerbation of asthma and cholestatic jaundice.

04 — Cycloserine

  • Mechanism of action: cell wall synthesis inhibitor acting at an earlier stage, by interfering with the formation of D-Ala containing peptidoglycan precursors.
  • Distribution: can cross the blood-brain barrier and the placenta.
  • Half-life: 10 hours.
  • Spectrum of activity: effective against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
  • Indication: second line drug in tuberculosis.
  • Adverse effects requiring monitoring
    • Dose-related CNS side effects
    • Folate and B12 deficiency
    • Elevated serum aminotransferase levels
  • It is generally reserved for situations where its benefit outweighs its risk.
Key Differentiator — Where Each Agent Hits the Wall Pathway Fosfomycin: earliest step of peptidoglycan synthesis.
Cycloserine: early, blocks formation of D-Ala containing precursors.
Vancomycin and teicoplanin: late, cap the finished D-Ala-D-Ala precursor outside the membrane.
Beta-lactams: last step, block transpeptidase cross-linking.
Daptomycin and polymyxins: not the wall at all — they disrupt the membrane.
Figure 7. Summary of Beta-Lactam and other cell wall and membrane active antibiotics. Lecturer's PPT · page 29
What to notice: the table is grouped by subclass — penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, monobactams, glycopeptide and lipopeptide. Read across one row and you get the same five columns each time — mechanism, effect, clinical application, pharmacokinetics and toxicity. Key rows to anchor are penicillin G with rapid renal clearance and a half-life around 30 minutes, cefazolin as the surgical prophylaxis agent with poor CNS penetration, imipenem-cilastatin with the seizure warning in renal failure at high doses, aztreonam with no cross-allergenicity to penicillins, vancomycin with trough targets and red man syndrome, and daptomycin that is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant and therefore cannot treat pneumonia.

Organ System Toxicities Across the Cell Wall Agents

Organ system toxicities as summarised on page 6
Organ systemAgent and effect
Central nervous systemHigh-dose imipenem and penicillins can provoke severe seizures and encephalopathy, especially in patients with renal dysfunction.
OticVancomycin carries a risk of ototoxicity — tinnitus, vertigo and hearing loss.
Risk is heavily linked to severe renal impairment.
Hepatic and biliaryCeftriaxone displaces bilirubin, giving a risk of kernicterus in neonates.
Ceftriaxone can precipitate with calcium, giving biliary pseudolithiasis.
Oxacillin is linked to hepatitis.

Red Flags and Kinetic Exceptions

The baseline rule and the exceptions that break it page 6

  • Baseline rule
    • Most beta-lactams are cleared rapidly with a half-life under 1 hour by the kidneys.
    • 10 percent by glomerular filtration and 90 percent by active tubular secretion.
  • Pharmacokinetic hack
    • Probenecid competitively blocks active tubular secretion, intentionally increasing serum concentrations and prolonging the half-life of penicillin.
  • Biliary exceptions — no renal dose adjustment generally needed
    • Nafcillin
    • Oxacillin
    • Ceftriaxone
    • These drugs are cleared primarily by biliary excretion into the GI tract.
  • Vancomycin management
    • About 90 percent is cleared by glomerular filtration.
    • Strict TDM is required.
    • Target trough 15 to 20 mcg per mL for severe MRSA infections.
    • Oral vancomycin is used for C. difficile colitis because it is not systemically absorbed.
Must Know — Clinical Considerations Before Prescribing Antimicrobial selection is not simply about which drug kills the organism.
Always consider renal function, hepatic function, allergy history, concomitant medications and patient-specific toxicity risk.
When prescribing a renally eliminated drug, ask three questions.
What is the patient's renal function?
Does the dose need renal adjustment?
Does the drug require therapeutic monitoring, such as vancomycin?

Tab Summary

The remaining wall and membrane agents

  • Mapped by where they cut the assembly line
    • Fosfomycin — MurA, the earliest cytoplasmic step
    • Cycloserine — D-alanine racemase and ligase
    • Bacitracin — bactoprenol recycling, the lipid carrier
    • Vancomycin — the D-Ala-D-Ala substrate
    • Beta-lactams — the final transpeptidase cross-link
  • Membrane agents sit outside that line entirely
    • Daptomycin depolarizes the Gram-positive membrane and is rapidly bactericidal.
    • Polymyxins bind LPS in Gram-negatives and are salvage therapy.
  • Red flags attached to each
    • Daptomycin — never for pneumonia, and check CPK.
    • Polymyxins — nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity.
    • Bacitracin — topical only, because systemic use is nephrotoxic.
    • Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin — urinary indications only.

III — Protein Synthesis Inhibitors: Overview of Ribosomal Targets

Why bacterial ribosomes are good drug targets, and exactly where each class binds on the 30S and 50S subunits.

The Class in One Card

Bacteriostatic ribosomal inhibitors page 7

  • These are antimicrobial agents that primarily inhibit bacterial protein synthesis.
  • Most of them are bacteriostatic.
    • They do not directly kill bacteria.
    • They stop bacterial growth and replication, allowing the host immune system to clear the infection.
  • Major ribosomal inhibitors
    • Tetracycline
    • Macrolides
    • Clindamycin
    • Chloramphenicol
    • Linezolid
Must Know — The Lecture Mnemonic "Buy AT 30, CELL for 50."
AT — Aminoglycosides and Tetracyclines are 30S inhibitors.
CELL — Chloramphenicol, Erythromycin, Linezolid and Lincosamides are 50S inhibitors.

A. Selective Toxicity

Why bacterial ribosomes are good targets page 7

  • Bacteria have 70S ribosomes composed of a 30S and a 50S subunit.
  • Human cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, composed of 40S and 60S subunits.
    • This structural difference allows antibiotics to selectively bind bacterial ribosomes while generally sparing human protein synthesis.
  • However, mitochondria also have 70S ribosomes.
    • This explains why some ribosomal inhibitors cause toxicity, especially with prolonged use and high doses.

01 — Prokaryotic 70S target page 7

  • High therapeutic index.
  • Subunit split: bacterial ribosomes consist of a small 30S subunit and a large 50S subunit.
  • Precise targeting: conserved rRNA folds and distinct ribosomal proteins allow selective binding of drugs.
  • Bacteriostatic arrest: reversible binding halts translation without killing the host cell, relying on intact immune defenses to clear bacteria.

02 — Eukaryotic 80S exclusions

  • Structural protection through different subunits, 40S and 60S.
  • Steric resistance: structural variations in host rRNA and auxiliary translation factors prevent binding.
  • Spare host machinery: mammalian protein synthesis is protected from drug-induced arrest at therapeutic levels.

B. Target 30S — Tetracycline versus Aminoglycoside

These agents interfere with the smaller 30S subunit by disrupting the initiation complex or by blocking transfer RNA binding. The general rule stated in the lecture is that 30S drugs affect early decoding, while 50S drugs affect elongation or initiation.

Two very different outcomes at the same subunit page 7
FeatureTetracyclines, for example doxycyclineAminoglycosides, for example gentamicin
BindingReversibleIrreversible
Site and actionBlocks aminoacyl-tRNA attachment to the A-site.
Binds highly conserved sequences of the 16S rRNA.		Binds the 16S rRNA near the active A-site and disrupts structural integrity.
Causes misreading of mRNA.
ConsequencePeptidyl transfer cannot occur without a loaded A-site, so chain elongation halts.Abnormal proteins are made, some of which damage the bacterial membrane.
EffectBacteriostatic.
Protein synthesis resumes immediately on drug withdrawal.		Rapidly bactericidal.
Cell integrity is compromised, forcing cell death and osmotic lysis.
Figure 8. Tetracycline blocking the A site. page 7
What to notice: the P site holds the nascent polypeptide chain while the incoming aminoacyl-tRNA tries to enter the A site. Tetracycline sits exactly at that acceptor site on the 30S subunit, so the new amino acid can never dock and the chain stops growing.

Tetracycline action in detail

  • Bacteriostatic action via reversible blockade.
  • Binding target: reversibly binds the 30S ribosomal subunit.
  • Specific site: interferes with the A-site, the aminoacyl-tRNA acceptor site, by physically blocking tRNA binding, so aminoacyl-tRNA cannot enter.
  • Mechanistic outcome: prevents entry of new amino acids into the A-site, which halts protein chain elongation. Since the ribosome cannot add new amino acids, protein synthesis stops.
  • Nature of effect: purely bacteriostatic. Protein synthesis resumes immediately upon drug withdrawal.

Aminoglycoside action in detail

  • Bactericidal damage via proofreading impairment.
  • Subunit target: binds irreversibly to the 30S subunit to disrupt structural integrity, causing misreading of mRNA and abnormal proteins.
  • Codon mismatching: impairs the accuracy of codon-anticodon matching, producing faulty protein synthesis.
  • Membrane disruption: defective proteins insert directly into the cytoplasmic membrane, destroying its barrier function.
  • Nature of effect: rapidly bactericidal, with cell death and osmotic lysis.

C. Interrupting Early-Stage Translation at the 16S rRNA

Tetracycline — reversible and static

  • Subunit docking: tetracyclines including doxycycline and minocycline bind reversibly to highly conserved sequences of the 16S rRNA on the 30S subunit, blocking aminoacyl-tRNA from reaching the A site.
  • tRNA exclusion: by occupying this locus they sterically block aminoacyl-tRNA from accessing the acceptor A-site on the mRNA-ribosome complex.
  • Bacteriostatic arrest: peptidyl transfer cannot occur without a loaded A-site, so chain elongation halts and growth is suppressed.

Aminoglycosides — cationic and lethal

  • Cationic outer pore entry: positively charged aminoglycosides attach to negatively charged LPS, forming large outer membrane pores to penetrate the envelope.
  • Oxygen-dependent transport: crossing the inner cytoplasmic membrane requires active transport powered by the proton motive force, which needs aerobic conditions.
    • This is why they are ineffective against anaerobes.
  • Codon misreading once inside: binds the 16S rRNA of the 30S subunit near the active A-site, inducing mRNA misreading and premature translation termination.

D. Target 50S Ribosomal Subunit

Table 8. Protein synthesis inhibitors acting on 50S ribosomal subunits page 7
Antibiotic classExamplesMechanism of actionEffect
MacrolidesAzithromycinBinds to 50S, blocking polypeptide elongationBacteriostatic
LincosamidesClindamycinSimilar mechanism to macrolides, inhibiting protein synthesisBacteriostatic
ChloramphenicolChloramphenicolBinds to 50S, inhibits peptidyl transferase activityBacteriostatic
OxazolidinonesLinezolidPrevents formation of the 70S initiation complexBacteriostatic

E. Targeting the 23S rRNA to Block Ribosomal Elongation

1Macrolides and lincosamides — translocation arrest.
Bind the 23S rRNA peptidyl transferase center. Halt translocation at an early stage, triggering the premature detachment of incomplete peptide chains. Lincosamides such as clindamycin share a similar overlapping binding locus.
▼
2Chloramphenicol — peptidyl transferase blockade.
Also binds the 50S subunit but directly inhibits peptidyl transferase, preventing peptide bond formation. It binds conserved sequences in the peptidyl transferase cavity of the 23S rRNA, blocking aminoacyl-tRNA binding to the A-site.
▼
3Oxazolidinones — initiation complex prevention.
Suppress 70S initiation complex assembly. Linezolid is a novel, completely synthetic class that interacts with peptidyl-tRNA and binds the 23S rRNA to arrest early peptide initiation, stopping protein synthesis at the earliest phase.

The 50S Ribosomal Blockade — Two Contrasting Binding Targets

Peptide exit tunnel block page 9

Macrolides and lincosamides such as clindamycin

  • Specific binding site: bind specific nucleotides within the 50S subunit, near the peptidyltransferase center.
  • Exit tunnel obstruction: physically block the polypeptide exit tunnel, preventing elongation of the newly formed peptide chain.
  • Translocation arrest: prevent translocation of tRNA from the A-site to the P-site.
  • Overlapping targets: because macrolides, lincosamides and streptogramins share overlapping exit tunnel sites, cross-resistance develops simultaneously.

Peptidyl transferase block page 9

Chloramphenicol, the drug of last resort

  • Enzyme targeting: binds specific nucleotides of the 50S subunit to directly inhibit peptidyl transferase activity, preventing peptide bond formation.
  • Peptide bond interruption: reversibly blocks the formation of peptide bonds between amino acids.
  • Ribosome inactivation: prevents chain elongation and freezes translation progression.
  • Mitochondria overlap: also inhibits eukaryotic mitochondrial peptidyl transferase, which is a 70S system, causing severe host toxicities. This is the key concern of the drug.
Clinical Cue — Quick Orientation Before the Drug Tabs Blocks the A site on 30S reversibly → tetracycline.
Misreads mRNA at 30S irreversibly → aminoglycoside.
Blocks the exit tunnel and translocation on 50S → macrolide and clindamycin.
Blocks peptidyl transferase on 50S → chloramphenicol.
Blocks assembly of the 70S initiation complex → linezolid.

Tab Summary

How to hold the ribosome block together

  • The selectivity argument
    • Bacteria use a 70S ribosome, built from 30S and 50S.
    • Human cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S.
    • Mitochondrial ribosomes resemble bacterial ones, which explains linezolid marrow and optic toxicity.
  • Split by subunit
    • 30S — aminoglycosides, which are cidal, and tetracyclines, which are static.
    • 50S — macrolides, clindamycin, chloramphenicol, linezolid and streptogramins.
  • Split by step of translation
    • Initiation — aminoglycosides and linezolid
    • tRNA delivery to the A site — tetracyclines
    • Peptide bond formation — chloramphenicol
    • Translocation — macrolides and clindamycin
  • The mnemonic to carry forward
    • Buy AT 30, CELL for 50.

IV — Tetracyclines

Broad-spectrum, bacteriostatic, actively concentrated inside bacteria, and defeated by two very different resistance tricks.

Orientation

The class in the lecturer's words page 8

  • Tetracyclines are broad spectrum, bacteriostatic antibiotics.
    • Examples — tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline and tigecycline.
  • They enter bacterial cells and bind the 30S subunit, preventing aminoacyl-tRNA from attaching to the mRNA-ribosome complex.
  • Clinically they are useful for atypical organisms such as chlamydia, rickettsia and some spirochetes.
  • Doxycycline is very popular because it is useful as a prophylactic against leptospirosis.
  • Adverse effect themes: GI upset, photosensitivity, effects on teeth and bones, and contraindication in pregnancy and young children.

Introduction page 8

  • Origin
    • First isolated from soil bacteria, the Actinomycetes.
  • Spectrum observed at discovery
    • Very broad spectrum, reaching even protozoa and anaerobes.
    • Covers both Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms.
  • Physical properties of the semi-synthetic agents
    • Water soluble.
    • Bitter in taste.
  • Effect
    • Bacteriostatic, so host immunity must finish the work.

Antimicrobial spectrum

  • Conventional bacteria
    • Cocci, both Gram-positive and Gram-negative
    • Bacilli
  • Organisms with unusual cell envelopes
    • Spirochetes
    • Mycoplasma, which has no cell wall and therefore escapes beta-lactams
    • Actinomyces

Classification by duration of action page 8

  • Short acting, 6 to 8 hours
    • Tetracycline
    • Chlortetracycline
    • Oxytetracycline
  • Intermediate acting, 12 hours
    • Demeclocycline
    • Methacycline
  • Long acting, 16 to 18 hours
    • Doxycycline
    • Minocycline
    • Tigecycline

Mechanism of Action and Resistance

Mechanism of action page 8

  • Tetracycline enters bacterial cells by passive diffusion and active transport.
  • It binds the 30S ribosomal unit and inhibits binding of aminoacyl-tRNA to the acceptor site on the mRNA-ribosome complex.
  • As a result the cell is unable to grow or replicate further.

Mechanism of resistance page 8

  • Bacteria modify entry systems to prevent the entry of tetracycline.
  • Efflux of tetracycline to reduce cytoplasmic concentration.
  • Mutations at the ribosomal subunit site.
  • Monooxygenase enzyme inactivates tetracycline by a hydroxylation reaction.

B. Tetracycline Translation Arrest — Step by Step

1Entry and concentration — active accumulation.
Passive diffusion carries the drug across the outer membrane of Gram-negative pathogens.
Active transport then lets susceptible bacteria concentrate the drug intracellularly, achieving high target-site levels.
▼
2Ribosomal binding — reversible attachment.
Reversibly binds specific pockets on the bacterial 30S subunit and positions itself to block access to the A-site of the translation complex.
▼
3tRNA exclusion — the blockade.
Acts as a physical barrier stopping aminoacyl-tRNA from associating with the ribosome.
The anticodon cannot bind the matching codon on the mRNA strand.
▼
4Translation stop — polypeptide arrest.
Prevents addition of new amino acid residues to the growing chain.
Reversible arrest — halts translation and replication without destroying the existing cell wall structure.

C. Resistance Genetics

01 — Active efflux pumps page 8

  • Tet(AE) and Tet(K) transporters pump tetracycline out of the cell, preventing adequate intracellular drug levels.
  • Gram-negative pumps: Tet(AE) actively pumps out older tetracyclines — tetracycline, doxycycline and minocycline — but cannot export tigecycline.
  • Gram-positive pumps: Tet(K) is found primarily in staphylococci, mediating resistance to tetracycline.
  • Net effect: a chemical shield that prevents the drug from reaching therapeutic levels inside the cell.

02 — Ribosomal protection page 8

  • Tet(M) protection proteins bind the ribosome and dislodge tetracycline from its target site, allowing protein synthesis to continue.
  • Structural protection: Tet(M) cytoplasmic proteins bind the bacterial ribosome.
  • Physical dislodgement: Tet(M) directly binds and releases tetracycline from its 30S target pocket.
  • Preserved translation: protein synthesis continues unaffected even at high antibiotic concentrations.

03 — Overcoming resistance with tigecycline page 8

  • Tigecycline is a semisynthetic glycylcycline.
  • Structural modification: features a bulky 9-t-butylglycylamido side chain derived from minocycline.
  • Steric shielding: the side chain prevents recognition and export by standard active efflux pumps, and allows binding even when ribosomal protection proteins are present.
  • Unhindered binding: overcomes Tet(M) protection proteins, restoring broad-spectrum 30S blockade.
Key Differentiator — Two Resistance Routes, One Solution Efflux removes the drug from the cell.
Ribosomal protection leaves the drug inside but kicks it off the ribosome.
Tigecycline defeats both, because its bulky side chain is not recognised by the pumps and is not displaced by Tet(M).

Clinical Uses

First choice drug for page 8

  • Respiratory and atypical infections
    • Atypical pneumonia
  • Enteric and zoonotic infections
    • Cholera
    • Brucellosis
    • Plague
  • Vector-borne and spirochetal infections
    • Relapsing fever
    • Dropping Mountain Fever, as named in the lecture

Second choice drug for page 8

  • Toxin-producing and spore-forming organisms
    • Tetanus
    • Anthrax
  • Sexually transmitted infections
    • Gonorrhea and syphilis
  • Respiratory indications
    • Pneumonia
    • Prophylactic use for COPD
  • Empiric situations
    • Imperial therapy, as written in the lecture, meaning treatment started before the organism is known

D. Clinical landmarks and pharmacokinetics page 8

  • Atypical pathogens: primary drugs for Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia and Rickettsia, including Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
  • Specific niches: Vibrio cholerae, plague, tularemia, brucellosis and spirochetes such as Lyme disease.
  • Pharmacokinetics
    • Doxycycline and minocycline are well absorbed orally.
    • Tigecycline is IV only, for complicated skin and soft tissue infections.
  • Elimination pathways: doxycycline is primarily eliminated non-renally via feces, requiring no renal dose adjustment.

Adverse Effects, Contraindications and Safety

Must Know — Who Must Not Receive Tetracyclines Cation chelation and tissue binding limit tetracyclines in specific populations.
Contraindicated in pregnant women, lactating mothers and children under the age of 8.

Mechanism-based adverse effects page 9

  • Calcium chelation
    • Tetracyclines chelate divalent and trivalent cations — Ca2+, Mg2+, Fe2+ and Al3+ — preventing absorption when taken with dairy, antacids or iron.
  • Tissue binding and discoloration
    • Bind tightly to newly forming bone and teeth, causing permanent brown enamel discoloration and bone growth inhibition.
  • Pediatric contraindication
    • Strictly avoided in children younger than 8 years and throughout pregnancy.
  • Additional risks
    • Demeclocycline causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
    • Older agents carry risks of phototoxicity and hepatic necrosis at high doses.

Full side effect list from the lecture page 8

  • Hepatic and gastrointestinal
    • Liver — jaundice and hepatic cell necrosis
    • Upper GI — epigastric pain, nausea, oesophageal ulcer and odynophagia
    • Lower GI — diarrhea and superinfection from microbiome disruption
  • Renal
    • Fanconi syndrome, described in the lecture as kidney failure
    • Classically linked to expired or degraded tetracycline
  • Metabolic
    • Antianabolic action, which raises blood urea nitrogen
    • Diabetes insipidus
  • Vestibular
    • Nystagmus, ataxia and vertigo
    • Most associated with minocycline
  • Allergic and dermatologic
    • Hypersensitivity reactions
    • Photosensitivity, so counsel on sun exposure

Aminoglycosides in Contrast — The Lecture's Bridge Note

  • Include drugs such as gentamicin, amikacin, tobramycin and streptomycin.
  • Bactericidal and bind the 30S subunit irreversibly, causing misreading of mRNA.
  • Especially useful against aerobic Gram-negative organisms and often used in severe infections such as sepsis, endocarditis and complicated intra-abdominal infections.
Must Know — Aminoglycoside Triad of Toxicity Nephrotoxicity.
Ototoxicity.
Neuromuscular blockade.

Tab Summary

Tetracyclines condensed

  • Mechanism and effect
    • Reversibly bind 30S and block aminoacyl-tRNA docking at the A site.
    • Bacteriostatic and exposure-dependent.
  • Spectrum niche
    • Strongest for organisms that beta-lactams cannot reach — atypicals, rickettsiae, chlamydiae and spirochetes.
    • Also CA-MRSA, cholera, brucellosis and plague.
  • Resistance
    • Efflux through Tet(A-E) and Tet(K)
    • Ribosomal protection through Tet(M)
    • Enzymatic inactivation
    • Tigecycline was designed to evade efflux and ribosomal protection.
  • Administration rules
    • Separate from iron, calcium, antacids and dairy, because of chelation.
    • Take with water and stay upright, to prevent oesophageal ulceration.
  • Restrictions and the exception
    • Avoid under 8 years and in pregnancy.
    • Doxycycline is still used for life-threatening rickettsial disease.

V — Macrolides and Ketolides

Complex polyketides that interfere with ribosomal translocation and exit tunnel transit, with two safety themes — CYP inhibition and QTc prolongation.

01 — Macrolide Structure

  • Polyketide core: a large macrocyclic lactone ring of 14, 15 or 16 atoms attached to deoxy sugars.
    • Mechanistically they bind reversibly to the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit.
  • Source: naturally produced as secondary metabolites by soil-dwelling strains of Streptomyces.
  • Class members: Erythromycin from 1952 and natural, plus the semisynthetics clarithromycin and azithromycin.

02 — Mechanism of Action: Translocation Blockade

1Subunit association. Reversibly bind specific bases on the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit.
▼
2Steric blockade. Obstruction of the exit tunnel prevents peptidyl-tRNA translocation from the A-site to the P-site.
▼
3Chain elongation arrest. Polypeptide growth halts, producing bacteriostatic translation inhibition.

03 — Ketolides: Telithromycin

  • Why they exist: ketolides such as telithromycin were developed to improve potency against resistant organisms.
  • Ring modification: a structural derivative substituting a 3-keto group for the standard L-cladinose sugar.
  • High affinity: binds at two distinct sites on the 50S subunit, providing superior potency against resistant strains.
  • Clinical warning: limited strictly to community-acquired pneumonia because of severe hepatotoxicity risks.

A. Macrolide Safety and Dynamics

Pharmacokinetic highlights page 9

  • Gastric sensitivity
    • Erythromycin base is destroyed by stomach acid, so it requires enteric coatings or stable salt formulations such as stearate or estolate. Erythromycin is acid labile.
  • Semisynthetic upgrades
    • Clarithromycin and azithromycin are acid-stable, with superior oral absorption and tissue levels.
  • Prolonged kinetics
    • Azithromycin has a massive volume of distribution and a 68-hour half-life, which allows short 3-day courses.
  • Excretion pathways
    • Highly concentrated in bile and cleared primarily in feces. Only clarithromycin requires renal adjustment.

Adverse effects and CYP interaction page 9

  • Cytochrome P450 inhibition
    • Erythromycin and clarithromycin are potent inhibitors of hepatic CYP3A4, dramatically increasing levels of statins, warfarin or theophylline.
  • Azithromycin advantage
    • Azithromycin lacks a 14-member ring, so it avoids CYP3A4 inhibition and the associated drug interactions. This is why it is more commonly used.
  • Cardiac safety risks
    • High concentrations block cardiac hERG potassium channels, causing QTc interval prolongation and lethal Torsades de Pointes.
  • Hepatotoxicity and GI
    • Erythromycin estolate can cause cholestatic jaundice.
    • Standard erythromycin stimulates stomach motilin receptors, commonly provoking severe GI upset.
Clinical Cue — If You See X, Think Y Macrolide with severe GI cramping → erythromycin acting on motilin receptors.
Macrolide with cholestatic jaundice → erythromycin estolate.
Macrolide with a statin or warfarin interaction → erythromycin or clarithromycin through CYP3A4.
Macrolide chosen to avoid interactions → azithromycin.

Tab Summary

Macrolides and ketolides condensed

  • Mechanism
    • Bind the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit and block translocation.
    • Usually bacteriostatic, and cidal at high concentration for selected organisms.
  • Spectrum
    • Atypicals, respiratory Gram-positives, Bordetella and Campylobacter.
    • Used in pertussis, chlamydial infection and MAC regimens.
  • Agent differences
    • Azithromycin — 68 hour half-life, long tissue persistence, fewest CYP interactions.
    • Clarithromycin and erythromycin — CYP3A4 inhibitors.
    • Erythromycin is also a motilin agonist.
  • Safety
    • QT prolongation and torsades.
    • Cholestatic hepatitis.
    • Reversible hearing effects.
  • Resistance
    • erm methylation of 23S rRNA
    • mef efflux pumps

VI — Clindamycin

Excellent anaerobic and antitoxin activity, balanced against the single most feared antibiotic-associated colitis.

A. Mechanism and Antitoxin Potency

  • Subunit binding
    • Binds the 50S subunit exit tunnel at a site overlapping macrolide and streptogramin targets.
  • Antitoxin effect
    • Inhibits ribosomal protein synthesis directly, which blocks production of bacterial superantigen exotoxins.
    • This makes it useful in severe toxin-mediated infections such as necrotizing fasciitis or toxic shock syndrome caused by streptococcus or staphylococcus.
  • TSS suppression
    • Shuts down exotoxins to prevent massive cytokine storms in streptococcal or staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome.
  • Host defense help
    • Inhibits bacterial synthesis of staphylococcal M-protein, which enhances phagocytosis by host leukocytes.

Clinical Indications and Niches

  • Anaerobic coverage
    • Highly active against Gram-positive and Gram-negative anaerobes such as Bacteroides fragilis and Prevotella.
    • Excellent anaerobic coverage, particularly for infections above the diaphragm.
  • Above-the-diaphragm niche
    • Key agent for aspiration pneumonia, lung abscesses and deep oral cavity infections.
  • Tissue penetration
    • Exceptional penetration into bones and joints, excellent for osteomyelitis, but it does not cross the blood-brain barrier into CSF.
  • Severe necrotizing fasciitis
    • Empiric triple-combination therapy pairs clindamycin with vancomycin and a beta-lactamase inhibitor.

B. Toxicity Warning — Black Box

Must Know — Pseudomembranous Colitis The most important toxicity of clindamycin is pseudomembranous colitis due to Clostridioides difficile.
It is a severe antibiotic-associated diarrheal disease and carries a black box warning.
1Gut flora disruption. Clindamycin aggressively suppresses protective intestinal microflora, eliminating competition for nutrients and removing the normal barrier that keeps C. difficile in check.
▼
2C. difficile selection. Colonisation with clindamycin-resistant strains of Clostridioides difficile is facilitated, allowing rapid overgrowth.
▼
3Exotoxin release. Proliferating bacteria produce two potent exotoxins that bind host intestinal receptors, causing cell damage and severe mucosal inflammation.
▼
4Pseudomembranes. Formation of pathognomonic pseudomembranes made of fibrin, inflammatory cells and necrotic debris.
Exam Trap — Risk Mitigation Reserve clindamycin for serious infections where alternative agents are clinically inappropriate.
Avoid it for viral or minor infections.
Remember the balance — excellent anaerobic and antitoxin activity, but a major risk of C. difficile colitis.

Tab Summary

Clindamycin condensed

  • Mechanism
    • Binds the 50S subunit near the macrolide site.
    • Blocks peptide transfer and translocation, and suppresses toxin production.
  • Where it earns its place
    • Gram-positive cocci but not enterococci.
    • Anaerobes above the diaphragm.
    • Adjunct for toxin suppression in severe group A streptococcal and clostridial disease.
  • The two facts that are always asked
    • Strongest association with C. difficile colitis.
    • Inducible resistance is revealed by the D-test when the isolate is erythromycin-resistant and clindamycin-susceptible.
  • Kinetics
    • Excellent oral absorption and tissue penetration, including bone.
    • Hepatic metabolism and poor CSF penetration.

VII — Chloramphenicol

A broad-spectrum agent with superb tissue penetration that is now a drug of last resort because of three signature toxicities.

Orientation and Introduction

Orientation page 10

  • Historically a broad spectrum antibiotic. It binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and inhibits peptide transfer, preventing peptide bond formation.
  • Despite broad activity and excellent tissue penetration, its use is now limited by serious toxicities.
  • It crosses the placenta and is secreted in breast milk, which matters because of the risk of toxicity in infants.
  • Today it is generally considered a drug of last resort.

Introduction and chemistry page 10

  • Initially obtained from the soil bacterium Streptomyces venezuelae. It is now commercially synthesised.
  • Bacteriostatic, but bactericidal at high concentration.
  • Crosses the placenta and is secreted in bile and milk.
  • A yellowish-white crystalline solid with an intensely bitter taste.
  • The aqueous solution is stable but needs protection from sunlight.
  • The nitro-benzene moiety is responsible for antimicrobial activity.

Mechanism of Action and Resistance

Mechanism of action page 10

  • Inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by preventing transfer of elongating peptide chains to the newly attached aminoacyl-tRNA at the ribosome-mRNA complex.
  • Attaches to the 50S subunit near the acceptor site and prevents peptide bond formation between the new amino acid and the nascent chain.
  • Binding is reversible, at nucleotides near the peptidyl transferase center, and translation is essentially frozen.

Mechanism of resistance page 10

  • Acquisition of an R plasmid encoding an acetyl-transferase, which inactivates chloramphenicol by acetylation.
  • Change in affinity at the 50S ribosome subunit site.
  • Decreased penetration of chloramphenicol.
Key Differentiator — When It Is Actually Cidal For most pathogens the action is bacteriostatic.
It shows bactericidal efficacy in highly sensitive strains — H. influenzae, N. meningitidis and S. pneumoniae.

Uses

Second choice drug for page 10

  • Instead of cephalosporins for
    • Pyogenic meningitis
    • Meningococcal meningitis
  • Instead of tetracycline for
    • Brucellosis
    • Rickettsial infections
  • Instead of erythromycin for
    • Whooping cough

As an alternative to clindamycin for page 10

  • Anaerobic infections and wound infections
  • Pelvic abscess and brain abscess
  • Intraocular infection and endophthalmitis
  • Enteric fever
  • Urinary tract infections
  • Topically in conjunctivitis

Clinical landmarks page 10

  • Extreme tissue penetration: exceptional tissue distribution, including excellent CSF levels for brain abscesses.
  • Historical utility: broad-spectrum coverage once made it a key choice for bacterial meningitis and typhoid fever, because of its excellent tissue and CSF penetration.
  • Modern role: strictly reserved for life-threatening multi-drug resistant pathogens such as VRE, or severe rickettsial diseases, when safer alternatives are not available.
