  • Veterinary niche: extensively used in veterinary medicine because toxicity profiles are significantly lower in animals.

C. Chloramphenicol Toxicities

Must Know — The Root of the Toxicity Host mitochondrial inhibition drives all three signature problems.
Bone marrow suppression.
Aplastic anemia.
Gray baby syndrome.
The three toxicities separated by mechanism, reversibility and timing page 10
ToxicityMechanism and outcome
01 Bone marrow suppression
Dose-dependent and reversible		 Mechanism: reversible inhibition of host mitochondrial ribosomes, which are 70S equivalents.
Respiration block: disrupts mitochondrial synthesis of key enzymes — cytochromes a, a3 and b.
Outcome: anemia, leukopenia or thrombocytopenia that resolves completely on discontinuation.
02 Idiosyncratic aplastic anemia
Irreversible and lethal		 Mutation risk: a rare, unpredictable bone marrow failure unrelated to dose or therapy length.
Nitroso side group: reactive intermediates interact with DNA, potentially causing mutagenic changes.
Clinical impact: often fatal, can develop weeks to months after therapy stops and may progress to leukemia.
03 Gray baby syndrome
Neonatal metabolic failure		 Enzymatic lack: newborns lack functional UDP-glucuronyl transferase and have immature glucuronidation, so they cannot metabolise the drug.
Toxic build-up: inability to conjugate leads to toxic blood accumulation.
Outcome: circulatory collapse with gray skin, blue lips, limp tone and cardiovascular shock, with high mortality.

Full side effect list from the lecture page 10

  • Hematologic: bone marrow suppression, aplastic anemia, agranulocytosis, pancytopenia, thrombocytosis
  • Hypersensitivity: rashes, fever, angioedema, atrophic glossitis
  • Irritative: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, pain at injection site
  • Other: superinfection and gray baby syndrome

Tab Summary

Chloramphenicol condensed

  • Mechanism
    • Binds the 50S peptidyl transferase center and blocks peptide bond formation.
    • Usually static, but cidal against selected meningitis pathogens.
  • Why it is still taught despite restriction
    • Broad spectrum, including anaerobes.
    • Excellent oral absorption and CSF penetration.
  • The toxicity that limits it
    • Dose-related reversible marrow suppression during therapy.
    • Idiosyncratic, delayed and often irreversible aplastic anemia, independent of dose.
    • Gray baby syndrome in neonates, from immature glucuronidation.
    • Optic and peripheral neuropathy.
  • Resistance
    • Chloramphenicol acetyltransferase, plus permeability and target changes.

VIII — Linezolid (Zyvox)

A fully synthetic oxazolidinone for resistant Gram-positives, with the strongest oral bioavailability in the lecture and a distinct set of toxicities.

Orientation

  • Linezolid is an oxazolidinone antibiotic.
  • Active mainly against resistant Gram-positive organisms, including MRSA and VRE.
  • It inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit and preventing formation of the initiation complex.
  • A major practical advantage is excellent oral bioavailability, which allows easy conversion from IV to oral therapy.
  • It carries important toxicities and interactions — thrombocytopenia, neuropathy, serotonin syndrome risk and lactic acidosis, plus peripheral and optic neuropathy with prolonged use.

Spectrum, dosage and pharmacokinetics pages 10 to 11

Spectrum of activity

  • MRSA
  • VRE
  • Streptococcus pneumoniae
  • No coverage for Gram-negative bacteria

Dosage

  • Adults — 600 mg IV or PO every 12 hours
  • Duration — typically 10 to 14 days, depending on the infection

Pharmacokinetics

  • 100 percent oral bioavailability, so switching from IV to PO is easy
  • Widely distributed with good lung and soft tissue penetration

Interactions, indications and warnings page 11

Drug interactions

  • SSRIs, MAOIs and TCAs — risk of serotonin syndrome
  • Avoid tyramine-rich foods, because linezolid acts as a weak MAO inhibitor
  • Monitor the platelet count

Indications

  • Nosocomial and community-acquired pneumonia
  • Skin and soft tissue infections
  • Resistant Gram-positive infections
  • VRE bacteremia

Side effects and warnings

  • Myelosuppression, especially thrombocytopenia beyond 2 weeks of use
  • Peripheral and optic neuropathy with prolonged use
  • Serotonin syndrome with SSRIs or MAOIs
  • Lactic acidosis

A. Oxazolidinone Initiation Blockade

1rRNA targeting. Linezolid binds the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit at a highly specific pocket during the initial translation phase. It is a completely synthetic class.
▼
2Initiation blockade. Prevents assembly of the functional 70S initiation complex, so the 30S and 50S subunits cannot properly join with fMet-tRNA.
▼
3Translocation arrest. Because initiation is blocked, protein synthesis cannot begin. There is no P-site transfer of the growing peptide chain. The effect is purely bacteriostatic.
▼
4Resistant Gram-positive efficacy. Highly active against severe aerobic Gram-positive pathogens and completely lacking activity against Gram-negative rods.

Note the contrast — macrolides and chloramphenicol interrupt an ongoing chain, whereas linezolid stops protein synthesis before it ever starts.

B. Linezolid Safety and Interactions

Clinical landmarks and spectrum page 11

  • Gram-positive focus: exceptional efficacy against drug-resistant Gram-positive cocci.
  • Target pathogens: approved for MRSA and vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium.
  • Severe infections: reserved for nosocomial pneumonia, community-acquired pneumonia and complicated skin structure infections.
  • Bioavailability: achieves 100 percent oral bioavailability, facilitating easy transition from IV to oral outpatient therapy. This is its key advantage, though toxicity risk limits prolonged use.

Adverse effects and drug warnings page 11

  • Reversible thrombocytopenia
    • Occurs in up to 30 percent of patients, particularly when therapy exceeds 2 weeks.
    • Prompts regular platelet counts through CBC.
  • MAO inhibition
    • Linezolid is a reversible, non-selective inhibitor of monoamine oxidase, both MAO-A and MAO-B.
  • Serotonin syndrome warning
    • Concomitant administration with SSRIs or other serotonergic antidepressants can cause lethal serotonin syndrome.
  • Neuropathies and lactic acidosis
    • Long-term use can cause peripheral neuropathy, irreversible optic neuropathy and lactic acidosis.
Clinical Pearls from the Lecture Excellent oral alternative to IV vancomycin.
Consider it for MRSA pneumonia or VRE infections.
Limit duration where possible because of hematologic and neurologic toxicity.

Summary of Class Pharmacology

  • Most of these agents are bacteriostatic. Clinical success therefore depends not only on the drug but also on host immune function and appropriate antimicrobial selection.
  • The key takeaway is to know, for each drug, the ribosomal target, the exact point at which it acts, the major clinical use, the resistance mechanism and the signature toxicity.
Figure 9. Summary of Class Pharmacology. Lecturer's PPT · page 30
What to notice: five rows, five columns. Track the ribosome target column first — tetracyclines at the 30S subunit, macrolides and clindamycin at the 50S exit tunnel, chloramphenicol at the 50S subunit, linezolid at the 50S 23S region. All five are listed as bacteriostatic in the clinical effect column. The resistance column pairs each drug with its escape route — efflux plus ribosomal protection for tetracyclines, 23S rRNA methylation by the erm gene plus efflux for macrolides and clindamycin with MLS-B cross-resistance, acetyltransferase for chloramphenicol, and point mutations in the 23S binding site for linezolid.

Tab Summary

Linezolid condensed

  • Mechanism
    • Binds the 50S subunit and prevents formation of the initiation complex.
    • Because it acts before the first peptide bond, there is no cross-resistance with other 50S agents.
  • Spectrum and role
    • Resistant Gram-positives, including MRSA and VRE.
    • No Gram-negative coverage.
    • Covers MRSA pneumonia, where daptomycin fails.
  • Kinetics
    • Nearly 100 percent oral bioavailability, enabling a clean IV to oral switch.
    • No routine renal dose adjustment.
  • Safety
    • Thrombocytopenia in about 30 percent beyond 2 weeks, so monitor the CBC.
    • Peripheral and optic neuropathy and lactic acidosis.
    • MAO inhibition, so review serotonergic and adrenergic drugs.

IX — Aminoglycosides: Chemistry, Uptake and Mechanism

Four concepts carry this whole section — how the drug gets in, what it does at the 30S subunit, why killing is concentration dependent, and why toxicity dictates dosing.

Orientation

Why this group is taught as a block page 11

  • Rapidly bactericidal, particularly against aerobic Gram-negative microorganisms.
  • Usefulness comes with important limitations, particularly nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.
  • Four major concepts to connect
    • How the drug enters the bacterial cell.
    • How it affects the 30S ribosomal subunit.
    • Why its killing is concentration dependent.
    • Why toxicity determines how we dose and monitor these drugs.

A. Overview

Agents and general behaviour page 11

  • Major agents: gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin, streptomycin, neomycin and related drugs.
  • Particularly useful against Gram-negative bacteria.
    • Activity against Gram-positive organisms is more limited.
    • It becomes useful when combined with cell-wall-active antibiotics.
  • Require energy-dependent and oxygen-dependent processes to enter the bacterial cell, which explains several important limitations of the group.

Introduction and chemistry page 11

  • In 1943 the first aminoglycoside was discovered — streptomycin, first obtained from the soil microorganism Actinomycetes.
  • It is a protein synthesis inhibitor and is now classified as bactericidal.
  • Can now be produced semi-synthetically in the laboratory.
  • Chemistry
    • Polybasic amino acids glycosidically linked with amino sugars. The sulfate form is more stable.
    • Alkaline in nature — neutralised in acidic medium and active in alkaline medium.
    • The actual structure remains unchanged when excreted in urine.

Classification page 11

  • Systemic aminoglycosides — streptomycin, gentamicin, kanamycin, tobramycin.
  • Topical aminoglycosides — neomycin and framycetin.

Uses — empiric therapy for

  • Endocarditis
  • Sepsis
  • Intra-abdominal infections
Must Know — Side Effects of the Class Ototoxicity.
Nephrotoxicity.
Neuromuscular blockade.

Mechanism of Action — the Multistep Sequence

Aminoglycosides mainly bind the 30S ribosomal subunit, but they also have affinity for the 50S and the interface site, and the result is inhibition of protein synthesis.

1The drug moves through bacterial porins and becomes trapped in the periplasmic space.
▼
2It moves into the cytoplasm by an Energy Dependent Phase 1 mechanism, which requires ATP and oxygen.
▼
3It binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and inhibits polysome formation because of misleading codons.
▼
4Chain formation of functional and structural proteins does not take place. Non-structural proteins incorporate into the cell wall, and the wall loses its integrity.
▼
5Energy Dependent Phase II starts, in which more aminoglycosides and other toxins move inside the cell and accumulate because energy is no longer needed.
▼
6Cell lysis of the bacterial cell takes place.

Mechanism of resistance stated in the overview page 12

  • Cell membrane-attached enzymes — adenylate and phosphorylate — attach groups to the aminoglycoside and change its structure.
    • Decrease in penetration of the aminoglycoside.
    • Decrease in affinity for the 30S ribosomal subunit.

B. Aminoglycoside Chemistry in Detail

  • Aminoglycosides consist of a central hexose ring attached to amino sugars through glycosidic linkages.
    • Streptomycin is different because its central nucleus is streptidine.
    • Gentamicin, tobramycin and amikacin contain 2-deoxystreptamine.
  • Numerous amino groups make these molecules highly polar and positively charged.
    • The pharmacological consequence is that they are very water soluble but poorly cross lipid membranes.
  • Activity is affected by the environment.
    • They work better at relatively alkaline pH and become less effective in acidic environments such as abscesses and infected tissue.
03 — Class-by-class architecture page 12
Core structureAgents and consequence
Streptidine nucleusStreptomycin.
Contains a unique streptidine ring.
Developed as a second-line antimycobacterial agent.
2-Deoxystreptamine coreGentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin.
The universal core of all systemically active agents.
The attachments determine vulnerability to modifying enzymes.
Polybasic subclassNeomycin, paromomycin, kanamycin.
Highly basic compounds with extreme nephrotoxicity.
This strictly limits systemic use and restricts them to topical or oral routes.
Figure 10. Summary of Structural Features of Aminoglycosides. Lecturer's PPT · page 30
What to notice: the left panel labels the hexose ring nucleus, which is either streptidine or 2-deoxystreptamine, with aminosugar rings attached by glycosidic linkages. The at-a-glance box repeats the four class facts — bactericidal, acts on the 30S subunit, concentration-dependent killing, best against aerobic Gram-negative organisms. The bottom strip explains the clinical consequence of chemistry — high water solubility, poor lipid crossing, and reduced potency in acidic tissue such as infected lungs and abscesses.

C. Three-Phase Uptake

1Phase 1 — Outer membrane passive diffusion.
Highly hydrophilic molecules cross the outer membrane of Gram-negatives rapidly and passively into the periplasmic space, through hydrophilic porin channels such as OmpF and OmpC.
This phase is concentration dependent and does not require energy or cellular respiration.
▼
2Phase 2 — Active cell membrane transport.
The drug must now cross the inner cytoplasmic membrane, which is the more important step.
It is an actively driven, energy-dependent process powered by the bacterial electron transport chain and the transmembrane electrochemical gradient, coupled to a respiratory proton pump.
This creates the major limitation — it requires aerobic cellular respiration.
▼
3Phase 3 — Oxygen dependence and its limits.
Under anaerobic conditions or low extracellular pH, the electrochemical gradient is severely reduced, fully blocking transport.
Consequently strict anaerobes are intrinsically resistant, and abscesses or necrotic tissue prevent drug entry.

Factors that limit aminoglycoside uptake page 12

  • Metabolic requirements of the bacterium
    • Oxygen required — the process needs aerobic respiration, which is why anaerobes are untouched.
    • pH dependent — acidic environments reduce uptake, as in abscesses.
  • Physical barriers to delivery
    • Porin expression — loss or mutation of porins decreases passive diffusion.
    • Biofilm and necrosis — limit penetration and reduce drug delivery.

D. The 30S Translation Blockade

Aminoglycosides attack the 30S subunit through three simultaneous ribosomal disruptions.

01 — Initiation complex blockade

  • Bind directly to 30S ribosomal subunit proteins.
  • This prevents assembly of the active 70S initiation complex.
  • It interferes with mRNA and tRNA docking.

02 — mRNA misreading and miscoding

  • Force the ribosome to misread mRNA codons. This is the most characteristic effect.
  • Non-functional aberrant proteins with incorrect amino acids are synthesised and inserted into cell membranes.

03 — Polysome breakup into monosomes

  • Interfere with ribosomal movement and cause disruption of polysomes.
  • Block ribosomal translocation along the mRNA strand.
  • Polysomes break up into non-functional isolated monosomes, which permanently freeze translation.

Why this is lethal rather than merely static

1Irreversible ribosomal binding. Other translation inhibitors bind reversibly. Aminoglycoside binding to the 30S is irreversible and halts cell machinery immediately.
▼
2Membrane permeabilization. Aberrant proteins become incorporated into the bacterial membrane, damaging integrity and causing leakage of ions and metabolites.
▼
3Self-feeding uptake cycle. Membrane damage further permeabilizes the cell, allowing a massive surge of aminoglycoside to flood the cytoplasm and shut down all remaining ribosomes. This lethal positive feedback loop drives rapid bacterial death.
Key Differentiator — Spectrum of Activity Excellent activity against: aerobic Gram-negative bacilli such as Pseudomonas and Enterobacteriaceae.
Limited activity against: Gram-positive bacteria, where they are used for synergy in severe infection.
Ineffective against: anaerobes, because uptake requires oxygen-dependent transport.
Figure 11. Summary of Mechanism of Action of Aminoglycosides. Lecturer's PPT · page 30
What to notice: the numbered left column is the same six-step killing sequence — entry into the cell through LPS binding, oxygen-dependent transport driven by the proton motive force, binding to the 16S rRNA of the 30S subunit near the A site, codon misreading, defective proteins damaging the membrane, and rapid bactericidal effect. The right column pairs the spectrum with clinical uses, and the bottom band lists the three adverse effects with their organ pictures — acute tubular necrosis, cochlear and vestibular damage, and acetylcholine-release blockade at the neuromuscular junction.

E. Penicillin–Aminoglycoside Synergy

Biophysical basis page 12

  • The problem being solved
    • Penetration into the bacterial cell wall is difficult for a highly polar drug.
  • What the partner drug does
    • Cell wall-active drugs — penicillins, cephalosporins and vancomycin — inhibit peptidoglycan synthesis.
    • The weakened wall stops acting as a barrier.
  • The resulting effect
    • Entry and uptake into the periplasmic space and cytoplasm are significantly enhanced.
    • The combined killing is more than additive, which is true synergy.
  • Where it matters clinically
    • Deep-seated or resistant infections, including selected endocarditis regimens.
Beta-lactam weakens the wall→ Aminoglycoside enters more easily→ Enhanced bactericidal killing
Clinical landmark uses of the combination page 12
Clinical situationCombination and rationale
Gram-positive endocarditisGentamicin combined with penicillin, ampicillin or vancomycin is the gold standard for achieving bactericidal killing in enterococcal or staphylococcal endocarditis.
Pseudomonas sepsisTobramycin combined with an antipseudomonal beta-lactam such as piperacillin-tazobactam or cefepime covers resistant strains and prevents rapid emergence of resistance in bacteremic patients.
Toxicity-mitigated alternativesBecause of aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity, dual cell-wall strategies such as ampicillin plus ceftriaxone are increasingly preferred in enterococcal endocarditis when possible, to avoid renal damage.
Must Know — Two Statements the Lecturer Paired Penicillin opens the door, aminoglycosides enter to attack.
This does not mean the combination is automatically preferred.
Still consider the increased potential for toxicity, especially nephrotoxicity.
Figure 12. Summary of the Synergistic Effect of the Penicillin–Aminoglycoside Combination. Lecturer's PPT · page 31
What to notice: the three numbered steps on the left are enhanced uptake, increased permeation and potent bactericidal action, illustrated as before, during and after synergy. The right panel lists the same three landmark scenarios covered in the table above, and the bottom grid pairs each clinical situation with its specific aminoglycoside, cell-wall partner and target pathogen. The closing line summarises the concept — cell wall-active agents open the door and aminoglycosides finish the job.

Tab Summary

Aminoglycosides part one

  • Mechanism in three effects
    • Blocks initiation complex formation.
    • Causes mRNA misreading, so faulty proteins are inserted into the membrane.
    • Disrupts polysomes into non-functional monosomes.
  • Why the killing is irreversible
    • The binding to 16S rRNA of the 30S subunit is irreversible.
    • Damaged membrane proteins let more drug flood in, which is a self-amplifying loop.
  • Uptake is the rate-limiting step
    • Requires oxygen-dependent active transport, so there is no anaerobic activity.
    • Reduced by acidic pH, porin loss, biofilm and necrotic tissue.
  • Synergy
    • Cell wall-active partners weaken the barrier and increase entry.
    • The combined effect is more than additive, which is true synergy.
  • Spectrum
    • Mainly aerobic Gram-negative bacilli.
    • Selected use against mycobacteria and enterococci in combination.

IX continued — Agents, Resistance, Dosing, Toxicity and Spectinomycin

How bacteria escape, which agent to choose, why once-daily dosing works, and the three adverse effects that define the class.

F. Bacterial Biochemical Escapes

Bacteria have three major ways of escaping aminoglycosides — enzymatic modification, decreased penetration and alteration of the ribosomal target.

01 — Enzymatic modification, the most important clinical mechanism page 13

  • R-plasmid encoded transferases modify the aminoglycoside through three chemical reactions.
    • Acetylation (AAC) — adds an acetyl group to amino groups.
    • Phosphorylation (APH) — adds a phosphate group to hydroxyl groups.
    • Adenylation (ANT) — adds an adenylyl group to hydroxyl groups.
  • Bacteria produce mobile genetic element encoded transferases that conjugate chemical groups onto the drug, and these modified drugs fail to bind the 30S subunit.
  • Amikacin and plazomicin were specifically designed to resist aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes.

02 — Decreased penetration

  • Porin mutations or deletions in the outer membrane prevent the early passive diffusion step.
  • Proton-pump disruptions affecting the electron transport chain disrupt the transmembrane electrical potential.
    • This lowers the proton motive force and completely blocks active energy-dependent transport.

03 — Alteration of the ribosomal target

  • Bacterial chromosomes mutate to protect the active target site.
    • Receptor deletion — single-step mutations alter or delete the specific protein receptor on the 30S subunit.
    • Binding site shift — drastically lowers binding affinity and renders the drug inactive.
  • This is observed readily during streptomycin monotherapy.
Must Know — Resistance Is Multifactorial Resistance arises through enzymatic drug inactivation, reduced entry or target change.
Overcoming resistance often requires combination therapy and antibiotic stewardship.
Figure 13. Summary of Biochemical Escapes from Aminoglycosides. Lecturer's PPT · page 31
What to notice: three numbered routes run left to right. Route 1 is the clinical chief — plasmid-encoded transferases — and the box beneath it names the three chemical modifications, AAC, APH and ANT. Route 2 splits into porin mutations on top and proton-pump disruption below, showing how the drug either cannot enter or cannot be transported without a proton motive force. Route 3 shows the 30S receptor being deleted or altered and the binding site shifting, with the note that this is readily observed during streptomycin monotherapy.

G. Specific Aminoglycoside Agents

01 — Gentamicin, the clinical workhorse

  • Natural mixture isolated from Micromonospora purpurea.
  • Gram-negative focus: highly active against aerobic Gram-negative bacilli including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Proteus, Serratia, Klebsiella and Enterobacter.
  • Gram-positive synergistic niche: uniquely combined with penicillin or vancomycin to achieve bactericidal killing against staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci.
  • Administration: intravenous by 30 to 60 minute infusion, or intramuscular.
    • Well absorbed after IM injection, with identical peak concentration achieved within 30 to 90 minutes.
  • Never as monotherapy for pneumonia
    • Aminoglycosides are severely impaired by the acidic, anaerobic environment of infected lung tissue.
    • Poor pulmonary tissue penetration makes them highly ineffective for pneumonia alone.
Must Know — Gentamicin Toxicity Profile Gentamicin carries a significant risk of irreversible vestibular damage, meaning vertigo and loss of balance.
It also causes reversible renal injury in the form of acute kidney injury.
Therapeutic drug monitoring is mandatory.

Gentamicin — mechanism, dosage and pharmacokinetics page 13

Mechanism of action

  • Irreversibly binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and inhibits protein synthesis.
  • Causes misreading of mRNA, leading to defective bacterial proteins.
  • Bactericidal with concentration-dependent killing.

Dosage

  • Adults — IV or IM 3 to 5 mg per kg per day divided every 8 hours.
  • Once-daily dosing — 5 to 7 mg per kg per day.
  • Neonates under 1 week — 4 mg per kg per dose every 24 hours.
  • Neonates over 1 week — 4 mg per kg per dose every 12 hours.
  • Children — 2.5 mg per kg per dose every 8 hours.

Pharmacokinetics and contraindications

  • Poor oral absorption.
  • Contraindicated in hypersensitivity.

Gentamicin — indications and adverse effects page 13

Indications

  • Severe Gram-negative infections
  • Septicemia
  • Meningitis
  • Pneumonia
  • UTIs
  • Peritonitis
  • Endocarditis with a beta-lactam
  • Neonatal sepsis
  • Osteomyelitis, especially Pseudomonas

Adverse effects

  • Nephrotoxicity — reversible
  • Ototoxicity — irreversible
  • Neuromuscular blockade — rare, enhanced with muscle relaxants
  • Allergic reactions

02 — Tobramycin, the antipseudomonal and inhaled option

  • Identical pharmacokinetics to gentamicin in absorption, renal clearance and half-life, which is 2.5 hours.
  • Pseudomonas superiority: slightly more active than gentamicin in vitro against Pseudomonas aeruginosa, making it the preferred choice for clinical Pseudomonas infections.
  • Cross resistance gap: cross-resistance occurs but is unpredictable, so separate laboratory susceptibility assays are mandatory.
  • Inhaled therapy for cystic fibrosis
    • 300 mg nebulizer formulation — a high dose solution of 300 mg in 5 mL, designed for inhalation in patients with cystic fibrosis complicated by chronic P. aeruginosa infection.
    • Localized action with reduced toxicity — nebulization deposits drug directly in the lower bronchi, average serum concentration stays extremely low at about 1 mcg per mL, sparing patients from systemic nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.
    • 28-day rotational regimen — twice-daily 300 mg in cycles of 28 days on therapy followed by 28 days off, to minimise resistance and balance safety.

Tobramycin — mechanism and spectrum page 13

  • Bactericidal and concentration-dependent.
  • Binds the 30S subunit, inhibits the initiation complex leading to mRNA misreading, and defective protein synthesis causes cell death.
  • Synergistic with beta-lactams, which increase cell wall permeability.
  • Effective against
    • Gram-negative bacilli — Pseudomonas aeruginosa, E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Proteus, Serratia
    • Some Staphylococcus aureus strains, including MRSA
  • Not effective against anaerobes, because uptake requires oxygen.

Tobramycin — indications and dosage pages 13 to 14

  • Severe Gram-negative infections, especially Pseudomonas
  • Septicemia
  • Lower respiratory tract infections
  • Meningitis with a beta-lactam
  • Peritonitis
  • Urinary tract infections
  • Eye infections using drops or ointment
  • Cystic fibrosis using the inhaled form

Dosage

  • Pediatrics — 5 to 7.5 mg per kg per day in 3 divided doses.
  • Serious Pseudomonas infections — up to 7.5 mg per kg per day.
  • Neonates — 2 to 2.5 mg per kg every 12 hours, adjusted to gestational age.
Must Know — Gentamicin and Tobramycin Share and Differ Both act at the 30S subunit.
Both show concentration-dependent bactericidal activity.
Both are primarily active against aerobic Gram-negative organisms.
Both need careful management because of renal toxicity, nephrotoxicity and vestibulotoxicity.
Tobramycin is distinct for its antipseudomonal role and its inhaled formulation.

H. Agents Designed to Overcome Resistance

Structural shielding in both amikacin and plazomicin changes the molecule so that bacterial enzymes have greater difficulty modifying it.

01 — Amikacin page 14

  • Semi-synthetic shielding: a semi-synthetic derivative of kanamycin A. Addition of a bulky side chain sterically shields the molecule from most bacterial modifying transferase enzymes.
  • Overcoming resistance: retains potent bactericidal activity against Gram-negative pathogens that are completely resistant to gentamicin and tobramycin.
  • Mycobacterial use: critical second-line agent for multi-drug resistant tuberculosis, always given in multi-drug combination regimens.
  • Mechanism: irreversibly binds the 30S subunit, causing mRNA misreading. Bactericidal with concentration-dependent killing.
  • Spectrum: broad, mainly aerobic Gram-negative bacilli — Pseudomonas aeruginosa, E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Proteus, Serratia. Less active against streptococci and anaerobes.
  • Dosage: adults 15 mg per kg per day IM in 2 divided doses, maximum 1.5 g per day. Children 15 to 22.5 mg per kg per day in 2 to 3 divided doses. Neonates 10 mg per kg then maintenance 7.5 mg.
  • Indications: severe Gram-negative infections, septicemia, hospital-acquired respiratory infections, intra-abdominal infections, UTIs, meningitis with other agents, neonatal sepsis.
  • Contraindications: known hypersensitivity to aminoglycosides, renal impairment, and pregnancy with caution as Category D.
  • Pharmacokinetics: parenteral use only.

02 — Plazomicin page 14

  • A sisomicin derivative with extensive structural modifications to resist enzymatic adenylation, acetylation and phosphorylation.
  • The newest FDA approved aminoglycoside.
  • Weapon against CRE infections
    • Retains clinical non-inferiority to meropenem.
    • Outstanding efficacy against highly resistant carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae.
  • Trough-only monitoring
    • Given strictly once daily at 15 mg per kg.
    • Uniquely requires trough-only therapeutic drug monitoring, targeting less than 3 mcg per mL, rather than peak and trough measurements.
  • Mechanism: binds irreversibly to the 30S subunit, causing mRNA misreading and inhibition of protein synthesis. Bactericidal.
  • Spectrum: broad activity against Gram-negative bacteria including MDR pathogens — Enterobacterales including CRE and ESBL producers, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii.

I. Strategic Dosing

Why aminoglycoside dosing is different page 14

  • Dosing differs from other drugs because of two properties.
    • Concentration-dependent killing
    • Post-antibiotic effect (PAE)
  • Because of these two effects, the therapeutic strategy is to
    • Give a large enough dose to achieve a high peak.
    • Allow the concentration to fall while the PAE continues to suppress bacterial growth.
    • Use extended interval or once-daily dosing.

Concentration-dependent killing

  • The rate and extent of killing increases as the peak concentration rises above the pathogen's MIC.
  • The critical parameter is the Cmax to MIC ratio, not simply keeping levels elevated for long periods.
  • Peak target for serious Gram-negative bacteremia — 8 to 10 mcg per mL for gentamicin and tobramycin.

Post-antibiotic effect

  • Continued suppression of bacterial growth and replication even after the drug level drops below the MIC or becomes undetectable in serum.
  • Aminoglycosides show a prolonged PAE against susceptible Gram-negative organisms, typically lasting 2 to 6 hours.
  • It is caused by sublethal persistent damage to the translation machinery from irreversible 30S binding, preventing rapid bacterial recovery for several hours.

Once-daily or extended interval dosing page 14

  • The entire daily dose is given as a single intravenous infusion rather than 2 to 3 divided doses — 5 to 7 mg per kg for gentamicin and tobramycin.
  • A large dose exploits concentration-dependent killing by achieving a massive peak Cmax and takes full advantage of the PAE.
  • Washout window: the dose is spaced to permit an 18 to 24 hour interval during which drug levels fall to negligible levels, allowing critical washout of tissues and reducing toxicity.
  • Sequence — high Cmax gives greater killing, PAE keeps suppressing as levels fall, then a long low-concentration window protects the kidney and inner ear.
Value Box — Toxicity Threshold and Therapeutic Drug Monitoring Threshold effect: toxicity is time-dependent and concentration-dependent and occurs when tissue concentrations cross a critical accumulation threshold over time.
Critical trough margin: a continuous trough above 2 mcg per mL is predictive of severe toxicity.
Once-daily dosing keeps trough levels safely below 1 mcg per mL for several hours.
Monitoring: for once-daily regimens, check troughs on day 2 or day 3 of therapy, aiming for a trough of less than 1 mcg per mL between 18 and 24 hours.
Overall rule: high peak, low troughs — improves bacterial killing while reducing accumulation and toxicity.
Figure 14. Once-Daily Dosing Overview. Lecturer's PPT · page 32
What to notice: the central concentration-time curve is the key image. The peak sits far above the MIC line for maximum killing, the shaded post-antibiotic effect region shows growth still suppressed after levels fall below the MIC, and the 18 to 24 hour washout window at the tail is what protects the kidney and inner ear. The right column repeats the three safety anchors — threshold effect, the trough above 2 mcg per mL danger line, and the TDM plan. The timeline strip at the bottom maps the whole cycle from peak at 0 to 1 hour through to the trough check at 18 to 24 hours.

J. Excretion Dynamics and Renal Adjustment

  • Excretion route: strictly cleared via the kidneys, and excretion is directly proportional to GFR, meaning creatinine clearance.
  • Half-life
    • Normally 2 to 3 hours.
    • In severe renal impairment it extends dramatically to 24 to 48 hours, so repeated doses can accumulate and produce toxicity. Dosing must be adjusted to renal function.
  • Poor dialysis clearance: only partially and irregularly removed by hemodialysis, about 40 to 60 percent for gentamicin, and even less effectively by peritoneal dialysis.
Dosing adjustments in renal impairment page 15
Situation or methodWhat to do
When once-daily dosing is avoidedOnce-daily dosing is avoided if creatinine clearance is below 60 mL per minute.
For a GFR above 60 mL per minute, once-daily dosing at 5 to 7 mg per kg is safe.
Below that threshold, traditional twice or thrice-daily dosing is recommended.
Traditional method A — increased intervalsKeep the dose constant at the standard mg per kg.
Significantly increase the dosing interval to allow clearance, moving from every 8 hours to every 12 hours to every 24 hours.
A longer interval gives the kidneys more time to eliminate the drug.
Traditional method B — reduced doseKeep the dosing interval constant, for example every 8 hours.
Significantly reduce the dose administered.
Formulas relate GFR to the size of the dose reduction.
Must Know — Before Giving an Aminoglycoside Know the patient's renal function before starting, and continue monitoring it during therapy.

K. Major Adverse Effects

01 — Nephrotoxicity page 15

  • Cortical accumulation: aminoglycosides selectively accumulate in the renal cortex, particularly in proximal tubular cells, despite low concentrations elsewhere.
  • Lysosomal rupture: uptake is mediated by saturable transport systems in proximal tubule cells, and over-accumulation triggers lysosomal swelling, rupture and cell damage.
  • Clinical incidence: reversible acute kidney injury occurs in 5 to 25 percent of patients receiving systemic aminoglycosides for longer than 3 to 5 days.
    • The AKI is generally reversible after discontinuation.
    • Risk increases with prolonged exposure.
  • Most nephrotoxic agents: neomycin, tobramycin and gentamicin. Plazomicin demonstrates lower AKI rates.
  • Earliest indicator of damage: a sudden increase in the trough serum aminoglycoside concentration itself, not a rising creatinine.
  • Potentiators: concurrent use of other nephrotoxic drugs such as loop diuretics, furosemide, vancomycin or amphotericin B severely potentiates renal injury.

02 — Ototoxicity page 15

  • Target pathology: progressive destruction of inner sensory hair cells, which is strictly irreversible, unlike nephrotoxicity.
  • Auditory damage: presents as tinnitus and high frequency hearing loss.
    • Main auditory toxins — neomycin, kanamycin and amikacin.
  • Vestibular damage: presents as severe vertigo, ataxia and loss of balance.
    • Main vestibulotoxins — streptomycin and gentamicin.
  • Mitochondrial point mutation: susceptibility to aminoglycoside-induced hearing loss is genetically determined and linked to maternal point mutations in mitochondrial DNA, for example the A1555G mutation.
  • Incidence and exposure window: occurs in 1 to 5 percent of patients, and risk increases significantly when therapy continues beyond 5 days or in elderly and GFR-impaired patients.
  • Loop diuretic amplification: concurrent furosemide or ethacrynic acid dramatically accelerates tissue accumulation, precipitating permanent deafness.

03 — Neuromuscular blockade page 15

  • Curare-like respiratory paralysis: at very high doses aminoglycosides produce curare-like neuromuscular blockade, leading to skeletal muscle weakness and respiratory paralysis.
  • Calcium antagonism: the drug blocks calcium channels at the presynaptic motor nerve terminal, preventing calcium-dependent exocytosis of acetylcholine vesicles.
  • High-risk scenario: historically occurred when massive doses of kanamycin, 3 to 5 g, or neomycin were instilled into the peritoneal cavity after surgery to wash abdominal wounds.
Must Know — Antidotes and Contraindication First-line antidote: calcium gluconate — prompt intravenous administration reverses the blockade by flooding the presynaptic terminal with calcium to restore acetylcholine release.
Second-line antidote: neostigmine — an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that maximises local acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction.
Myasthenia gravis: transmission is already impaired, and because aminoglycosides block presynaptic calcium channels they are strictly contraindicated and can precipitate a lethal respiratory crisis.

L. Spectinomycin

A related aminocyclitol alternative for resistant gonorrhea page 15

  • Structure: an aminocyclitol antibiotic, structurally related to aminoglycosides but lacking amino sugars and glycosidic bonds.
  • Protein synthesis blockade: binds reversibly to the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit to inhibit protein synthesis.
    • Like aminoglycosides it targets the 30S, but unlike them it is only bacteriostatic because binding is reversible.
  • Resistance profiling: resistant strains exist, but spectinomycin shows no cross-resistance with other major anti-gonorrheal agents.
  • Clinical landmark use: used almost exclusively as an alternative treatment for drug-resistant gonorrhea caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, or in patients with severe penicillin or cephalosporin allergies.
  • Not for pharyngeal gonorrhea: poor efficacy and high treatment failure rates in pharyngeal gonococcal infection, so it is not recommended for pharyngeal presentations.
  • Administration and safety: rapidly absorbed after a single intramuscular injection of 2 to 4 g. Pain at the injection site, fever and nausea are common. Nephrotoxicity and anemia are extremely rare.
Do Not Confuse — Spectinomycin Is Not an Aminoglycoside Same target: the 30S ribosomal subunit.
Different chemistry: aminocyclitol with no amino sugars and no glycosidic bonds.
Different binding: reversible rather than irreversible.
Different effect: bacteriostatic, not bactericidal.

Tab Summary

Aminoglycosides part two

  • Resistance
    • Acetyltransferases, phosphotransferases and nucleotidyltransferases modify the drug.
    • 16S rRNA target change and reduced entry or efflux.
    • Amikacin resists many modifying enzymes, which is why it is held in reserve.
  • Agent identities
    • Gentamicin — synergy workhorse, vestibular injury.
    • Tobramycin — better against Pseudomonas, nebulized in cystic fibrosis, cochlear injury.
    • Amikacin — broadest, cochlear injury.
    • Plazomicin — resistant Enterobacterales, trough-only monitoring.
  • Dosing strategy
    • Concentration-dependent killing, so the index is Cmax to MIC.
    • Post-antibiotic effect of 2 to 6 hours permits once-daily dosing at 5 to 7 mg per kg.
    • The 18 to 24 hour washout is what protects the proximal tubule.
  • Monitoring thresholds
    • Peak target 8 to 10 mcg per mL, with a ceiling below 10 mg per L for ototoxicity.
    • Trough above 2 mcg per mL predicts toxicity, and below 1 is the target.
    • Check levels on day 2 to 3, and adjust when creatinine clearance falls below 60.
  • Three toxicities
    • Nephrotoxicity as acute tubular necrosis, usually reversible.
    • Ototoxicity, cochlear or vestibular, usually irreversible.
    • Neuromuscular blockade, reversed with calcium gluconate then neostigmine, and contraindicated in myasthenia gravis.

X and XI — Antimetabolites: Sulfonamides and Trimethoprim

One pathway, two enzymes, two drugs. Blocking both converts two bacteriostatic agents into a bactericidal combination.

X — Antimetabolites and Nucleic Acid Synthesis Inhibitors

Why these two very different classes are taught together page 15

  • Sulfonamides and trimethoprim are folate antagonists.
  • Fluoroquinolones interfere with nucleic acid synthesis.
  • Even though the drugs are very different, both ultimately interfere with the ability of microorganisms to replicate.
  • Four recurring questions to focus on
    • What is the target?
    • Why is the target selectively toxic to bacteria?
    • How does resistance occur?
    • What toxicities limit clinical use?

A. Therapeutic targets — folate pathway antagonists

  • Metabolic precursor blockade: unlike mammalian cells, bacteria cannot absorb dietary folate and must synthesise tetrahydrofolic acid de novo to manufacture purines and DNA.
  • Competitive structural mimics
    • Sulfonamides mimic PABA to inhibit dihydropteroate synthase.
    • Trimethoprim mimics folic acid to block dihydrofolate reductase.
  • Sequential blockade synergy: when paired, sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim execute a sequential blockade that transitions individual bacteriostatic activities into a powerful bactericidal combination.

Fluoroquinolones as nucleic acid metabolism blockers

  • Mechanical replication blockade: selectively target the bacterial enzymes controlling mechanical stress and separation of double-stranded DNA during replication.
  • Dual enzymatic cleavage
    • Inhibit DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) to halt relaxation of positive supercoiling.
    • Inhibit topoisomerase IV to prevent decatenation of replicated chromosomes.
  • Rapidly bactericidal action: by trapping the DNA-enzyme cleavable complex, they induce double-stranded DNA breaks and immediate bacterial death.
Figure 15. Therapeutic Targets of Sulfonamides and Fluoroquinolones. Lecturer's PPT · page 32
What to notice: the slide is split deliberately. On the left, PABA feeds dihydropteroate synthase, which sulfonamides block, and then dihydrofolate reductase, which trimethoprim blocks, producing THF. On the right, topoisomerases introduce transient DNA breaks, fluoroquinolones stabilise the cleavable complex, and religation is prevented so double-strand breaks accumulate. Two critical targets, one combined goal — disrupt bacterial growth and survival.

XI.A — Sulfonamide Overview

Overview page 16

  • Synthetic antibacterial agents.
  • Primarily bacteriostatic when used alone.
  • The mechanism centres on inhibition of bacterial folate synthesis.
    • Bacteria must manufacture their own folate.
    • Blocking folate synthesis prevents production of the nucleotides needed for growth and replication.
  • Can be classified by duration of action.
  • Clinical uses have evolved considerably because resistance has become common, so one of the most important applications today is combination therapy, particularly sulfamethoxazole with trimethoprim.

Introduction and chemistry page 16

  • In 1930, G. Domagk used Prontosil, a dye, to treat septicemia.
  • In 1939 he was awarded the Nobel Prize.
  • The pioneer antibiotic to treat bacterial infections.
  • Sulfonamide antibiotics are synthetic and bacteriostatic.
  • Chemistry
    • The basic chemical entity is sulfanilamide.
    • N1 determines antibacterial action.
    • N4 determines pharmacokinetics and potency.
Figure 16. Sulfonamides with varying N1 substituents and the same N4 substituent. Katzung 16th Ed, Fig 43-1 · page 16
What to notice: compare sulfanilamide with p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) at the top. The two share almost the same shape, which is the whole basis of competitive inhibition. Below, sulfadiazine and sulfamethoxazole keep the same N4 amino group but carry different N1 substituents, which is what changes potency and pharmacokinetics between agents.

Classification and duration of action page 16

  • Short-acting — Sulfadiazine. Duration 4 to 8 hours.
  • Intermediate acting — Sulfamethoxazole. Duration 8 to 12 hours.
  • Long-acting — Sulfadoxine. Duration 7 days.
  • Other — Mafenide and Sulfacetamide.

Mechanism of action stated in the overview

  • Sulfonamide inhibits folate synthase, stops cell division and inhibits bacterial growth.
  • Trimethoprim in combination with sulfamethoxazole, known as cotrimoxazole, inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and blocks both steps in the folic acid synthesis pathway.

Mechanism of resistance, uses and side effects page 16

Resistance

  • Change in affinity of the enzyme.
  • Increased PABA, which antagonises sulfonamides.
  • Alternate pathway — bacteria use another route to form folic acid.

Uses

  • Urinary tract infection
  • Upper and lower respiratory tract infections
  • Bacterial diarrhea and dysentery
  • Prevention of pneumonia
  • Typhoid fever
  • Preventing infection on burnt skin

Side effects

  • Nausea, vomiting and epigastric pain
  • Crystalluria
  • Photosensitivity
  • Hepatitis by unknown mechanism
  • Hemolysis
  • Kernicterus

B. Folate Metabolism — the Reason for Selective Toxicity

  • Mammalian dietary import
    • Mammals completely lack the enzymes required for de novo folate synthesis.
    • Mammalian cells absorb preformed dietary folic acid, vitamin B9, using specialised high-affinity active transport proteins.
  • Bacterial transport deficit
    • Most pathogenic bacteria are entirely devoid of folate transport mechanisms and are impermeable to exogenous folic acid.
    • Consequently they must synthesise folate de novo from basic chemical precursors, including PABA.
  • Folate role in coenzyme production
    • Tetrahydrofolic acid (THF) is an essential carbon-donor coenzyme.
    • It is required for synthesis of thymidine, purines such as adenine and guanine, and methionine, which are the fundamental building blocks of bacterial DNA, RNA and proteins.
  • The two enzymes in sequence
    • Dihydropteroate synthase (DHPS) participates in producing the folate intermediate.
    • Dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) converts dihydrofolate into tetrahydrofolate.
Pteridine + PABA→ DHPS → Dihydropteroic acid, then DHF→ DHFR → Tetrahydrofolic acid (THF)→ Purines, thymidine, bacterial DNA

Study aid derived from Figure 17. Sulfonamides block the first arrow. Trimethoprim blocks the second arrow.

Key Differentiator — Why This Is Selectively Toxic Mammals simply absorb dietary folate.
Bacteria must construct folate themselves.
If we selectively block the enzymes that bacteria depend on and that humans do not use in the same way, we achieve selective antimicrobial toxicity.
Figure 17. Obligate Bacterial De Novo Folate Synthesis. Lecturer's PPT · page 16
What to notice: the two red inhibition bars. The upper one is sulfonamides competing with PABA at the early assembly step. The lower one is trimethoprim selectively blocking DHFR. The final output box is purines, thymidine and bacterial DNA production.
Figure 18. Summary of Folate Metabolism — Selective Toxicity. Lecturer's PPT · page 32
What to notice: the left column shows mammals lacking de novo folate enzymes and absorbing dietary folate through the proton-coupled folate transporter. The right column shows bacteria that cannot import folate and must run the six-step de novo pathway. The centre column marks the exact blocked steps for each drug.

C. Sulfonamide Mechanism of Action

Competitive antimetabolite action page 16

  • PABA structural nucleus
    • Sulfonamides possess a common chemical nucleus, a para-aminobenzenesulfonamide core, giving high structural similarity to PABA, the natural precursor substrate.
  • Competitive active-site binding
    • They bind reversibly and competitively to the active site of DHPS, physically blocking PABA from binding.
    • This halts production of dihydropteroic acid and prevents the normal substrate from participating in folate synthesis.
  • False substrate incorporation
    • Sulfonamides can also act as false substrates. The enzyme incorporates the sulfonamide instead of PABA, generating a non-functional dead-end pteridine-sulfonamide conjugate that cannot be processed further.
  • Bacteriostatic arrest
    • By preventing folate accumulation, sulfonamides halt cell division but do not actively kill existing cells, so as monotherapy they are strictly bacteriostatic.

Chemical characteristics and classes pages 16 to 17

  • Weak acids and solubility
    • Sulfonamides are weakly acidic compounds.
    • Solubility is significantly reduced in acidic environments below pH 5.5, which can lead to drug precipitation and crystalluria in acidic urine.
  • Pharmacokinetic actions
    • Modest tissue penetration.
    • Bind extensively to plasma albumin, competing with bilirubin.
    • Undergo hepatic N-acetylation and are excreted renally.
  • Short-acting agents
    • Sulfisoxazole is highly water-soluble, rapidly absorbed and excreted, making it useful for simple urinary tract infections.
  • Intermediate and long-acting
    • Sulfamethoxazole, with a half-life of 10 to 12 hours, is the intermediate standard.
    • Sulfadoxine is ultra-long-acting and is used in combination with pyrimethamine for malaria.
Figure 19. Summary of Sulfonamides Mechanism of Action. Lecturer's PPT · page 33
What to notice: the left panel puts the PABA and sulfonamide structures side by side and shows the sulfonamide entering the DHPS active site so that dihydropteroic acid is never formed, with the result labelled bacteriostatic when used alone. The right panel is the safety half — weak acids, low solubility in acidic urine leading to crystalluria with the advice to maintain hydration and alkaline urine, albumin binding that competes with bilirubin and risks kernicterus in neonates, hepatic N-acetylation and renal excretion.

D. Trimethoprim Mechanism of Action

Targeting the conversion to active folate page 17

  • Folic acid structural analogue
    • Trimethoprim is structurally similar to the pteridine portion of folic acid, which lets it target the enzyme that converts inactive folates into active forms.
  • Selective DHFR blockade
    • Binds reversibly and competitively to bacterial DHFR, halting reduction of dihydrofolic acid into THF and preventing formation of essential carbon-donor coenzymes.
  • Enzymatic selectivity
    • The enzyme is highly conserved, but bacterial DHFR is 4 to 5 orders of magnitude more sensitive to trimethoprim than the human enzyme, which is 10,000 to 100,000 times.
    • This is what ensures selective toxicity and allows safe clinical use.
  • Pyrimethamine parallel
    • Pyrimethamine is a related DHFR inhibitor with high affinity for protozoal DHFR, making it useful in protozoal infections such as malaria and toxoplasmosis.

Chemical properties and distribution page 17

  • Weak base dynamics
    • Unlike sulfonamides, trimethoprim is a weak base, which allows ion trapping in acidic environments and concentrates it in tissues more acidic than plasma.
  • Prostatic and vaginal penetration
    • Because of ion trapping, it reaches exceptionally high concentrations in prostatic and vaginal fluids, making it an ideal choice for bacterial prostatitis and vaginitis.
  • Unchanged renal clearance
    • Renally excreted and concentrated in the urinary and genitourinary systems.
    • 60 to 80 percent is excreted completely unchanged in urine, ensuring high bladder concentrations against urinary pathogens.
  • Plasma half-life sync
    • Plasma half-life of approximately 10 to 12 hours, matching the half-life of sulfamethoxazole at about 10 hours, which allows a stable fixed-dose ratio.
Figure 20. Trimethoprim Mechanism of Action — Selective DHFR Blockade. Lecturer's PPT · page 33
What to notice: the left side shows trimethoprim mimicking the pteridine portion of folic acid and occupying bacterial DHFR so that DHF cannot be reduced to THF, with the shield box stating bacterial DHFR is 10,000 to 100,000 times more sensitive than mammalian DHFR. The right column is the distribution story — weak base, ion trapping in acidic fluids, and the organ icons showing why the drug concentrates in kidney, prostate and bladder.

E. Sequential Blockade

The dynamics of blocking two steps in one pathway page 17

  • Definition: the combined action of two drugs that inhibit sequential enzymatic steps in a single metabolic pathway.
    • In folate synthesis, sulfamethoxazole first reduces intermediate production, and trimethoprim then inhibits the processing of what remains.
  • Transition to bactericidal power
    • Individually both are bacteriostatic and require host immunity to clear the pathogen.
    • Combined in a 5 to 1 ratio as TMP-SMZ or co-trimoxazole, the synergistic effect blocks folate synthesis so completely that it becomes bactericidal against susceptible strains.
  • Slower resistance evolution
    • A bacterium would need simultaneous rare mutations in both DHPS and DHFR to survive the combination.
    • Clinical resistance to TMP-SMZ therefore develops much more slowly than to either agent alone.
Alone versus combined page 17
RegimenEnzyme inhibitedResult
Sulfamethoxazole aloneEarly-stage dihydropteroate synthaseFolate levels fall slowly and bacteria halt division.
Bacteriostatic effect.
Trimethoprim aloneLate-stage dihydrofolate reductaseFolate reduction halts and cell division stops.
Bacteriostatic effect.
TMP-SMX combinationBoth enzymes, sequential double strikeComplete folate depletion shuts down DNA assembly.
Highly bactericidal.
Must Know — TMP-SMX, Two Hits, One Pathway First stop: sulfamethoxazole acting on DHPS.
Second stop: trimethoprim acting on DHFR.
Used alone, either drug is bacteriostatic. Used together they create a double strike on the same pathway.
The end point is loss of THF, loss of reduced one-carbon units, interruption of DNA assembly and an almost bactericidal antimicrobial effect.
Figure 21. Sequential Blockade — TMP-SMX Bactericidal Synergy. Lecturer's PPT · page 33
What to notice: the top pathway strip has two stop signs — an early blockade at DHPS that stops folate production at the start, and a late blockade at DHFR that prevents regeneration of active folate. The right boxes carry two numbers worth memorising — the 5 to 1 fixed ratio of sulfamethoxazole to trimethoprim, and the reason resistance evolves slowly, because mutations would be needed in both enzymes. The bottom row contrasts alone versus alone versus combined, ending in bactericidal.

F. Antifolate Resistance

General principles page 17

  • Bacteria employ plasmid-mediated synthesis of insensitive enzymes and PABA overproduction.
  • Antibiotic resistance genes can move horizontally between bacterial strains.
  • Genetic elements allow resistance traits to spread through a bacterial population.
  • The clinical consequence is treatment failure, particularly when empirical therapy is chosen without considering local susceptibility patterns.
  • Three broad principles of resistance
    • Change the target.
    • Overwhelm the inhibitor.
    • Reduce the intracellular drug concentration.

Sulfonamide resistance pathways

  • Mutated synthase targets
    • Plasmids transmit mutated genes encoding a modified DHPS that keeps normal affinity for PABA but has greatly reduced binding for sulfonamides.
  • Hyperproduction of PABA
    • Gene mutations cause PABA hyperproduction, sometimes up to 70-fold.
    • This massive excess of natural substrate outcompetes the sulfonamide at the active site.
  • Decreased drug accumulation
    • Plasmid-mediated changes in outer membrane porin structure or up-regulation of multi-drug efflux pumps prevent the drug from reaching inhibitory levels in the cytoplasm.

Trimethoprim resistance pathways

  • Mutated DHFR targets — the most common clinical mechanism
    • Plasmid-encoded genes construct a modified DHFR with vastly reduced affinity for trimethoprim, up to a 1,000-fold reduction.
  • Overproduction of DHFR
    • Promoter mutations cause massive overproduction of the normal enzyme, saturating the drug and maintaining enough active THF for survival.
  • Cross-resistance reality
    • Although resistance to the combination develops more slowly, plasmid-mediated transmission is common in Gram-negative bacilli such as E. coli, leading to rising resistance rates in community UTIs.
Figure 22. Summary of Antifolate Resistance — Enzyme Escape and PABA Overproduction. Lecturer's PPT · page 34
What to notice: both halves use the same three-step layout. On the sulfonamide side the steps are mutated DHPS with low sulfonamide affinity, PABA flooding that outcompetes the drug, and decreased accumulation through porin changes or efflux. On the trimethoprim side they are plasmid-encoded mutated DHFR, DHFR overproduction, and plasmid-mediated spread in Gram-negative bacilli with the clinical endpoint flagged as rising trimethoprim resistance in E. coli causing UTIs.

G. Clinical Use

Must Know — Where TMP-SMZ Remains Critical TMP-SMZ remains a critical choice for urinary, respiratory and pneumocystis infections.
Therapy should be guided by susceptibility, renal function, allergy history, electrolyte monitoring and drug interactions.

What to notice: six numbered indications surround the central tablet — uncomplicated lower UTI, PJP prevention and treatment, Nocardia as drug of choice, toxoplasmosis using pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine with leucovorin, community-associated MRSA skin infection and Listeria as a penicillin-allergy alternative. H. Antifolate Toxicity

Must Know — The Toxicity Headline Allergic rashes.
Bone marrow suppression.
G6PD hemolysis.
Neonatal kernicterus.

Sulfonamide toxicity and hypersensitivity page 18

  • Stevens-Johnson syndrome
    • The most feared reaction. Sulfonamides are classic triggers of SJS and toxic epidermal necrolysis, presenting as painful blisters and skin sloughing.
  • Crystalluria and hematuria
    • Drug precipitation in acidic urine can block renal tubules, causing severe pain and blood in the urine.
    • Prevented by maintaining high fluid intake and urine alkalinization.
  • G6PD deficiency hemolysis
    • In G6PD-deficient patients, sulfonamides provoke acute red blood cell oxidative stress, triggering hemolytic anemia.
  • Neonatal kernicterus
    • Sulfonamides displace bilirubin from albumin binding sites.
    • In the third trimester, free bilirubin crosses the newborn blood-brain barrier and deposits in the basal ganglia.
    • Contraindicated in late pregnancy.

Trimethoprim toxicity and AIDS sensitivity page 18

  • Megaloblastic anemia
    • By blocking DHFR, trimethoprim can cause folate deficiency, presenting as macrocytic megaloblastic anemia, leukopenia and thrombocytopenia.
  • Folinic acid rescue
    • These hematotoxic effects are completely prevented or reversed by supplemental folinic acid or leucovorin, which bacterial cells cannot absorb.
  • Hyperkalemia risk
    • Trimethoprim acts as a weak potassium-sparing diuretic, blocking epithelial sodium channels in distal tubules, which can cause significant hyperkalemia.
  • AIDS patient hypersensitivity
    • Up to 50 to 80 percent of AIDS patients given TMP-SMZ experience severe adverse reactions — high fever, painful rashes, profound leukopenia and diarrhea — requiring alternative therapy.
Clinical Cue — If You See X, Think Y Antibiotic plus Stevens-Johnson syndrome → think sulfonamide.
Antibiotic plus hemolysis in G6PD deficiency → think sulfonamide.
Antibiotic plus hyperkalemia → think trimethoprim blocking epithelial sodium channels.
Antibiotic plus megaloblastic anemia rescued by leucovorin → think trimethoprim.

Tab Summary

Antifolates condensed

  • The pathway being cut twice
    • PABA to dihydropteroate by dihydropteroate synthase, blocked by sulfonamides.
    • Dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate by dihydrofolate reductase, blocked by trimethoprim.
    • Tetrahydrofolate feeds purine, pyrimidine and amino acid synthesis.
  • Why the host is spared
    • Bacteria must synthesise folate, while humans absorb preformed folate.
    • Trimethoprim prefers the bacterial enzyme by 10,000 to 100,000-fold.
  • Sequential blockade
    • Mixed at 5 parts sulfamethoxazole to 1 part trimethoprim.
    • Matched 10 hour half-lives keep the ratio stable in serum.
    • Two static drugs become an often bactericidal combination.
  • Where it is the drug of choice
    • Pneumocystis jirovecii treatment and prophylaxis
    • Nocardiosis
    • Stenotrophomonas infection
    • CA-MRSA and uncomplicated UTI
  • Toxicity checklist
    • SJS and TEN, plus photosensitivity
    • Crystalluria and nephrotoxicity
    • G6PD hemolysis and kernicterus
    • Megaloblastic anemia, prevented with folinic acid
    • Hyperkalemia and a creatinine rise without true GFR loss

XII — Fluoroquinolones

Dual-enzyme DNA blockade, outstanding oral bioavailability, and a safety profile that now demands restraint.

A. Overview of Quinolones

Introduction page 18

  • Semi-synthetic bactericidal agents that interfere with bacterial DNA metabolism.
  • Spectrum is expanded as newer agents are developed.
  • They are metabolic pathway inhibitors of the cell.
  • Nalidixic acid, the first generation, had clear drawbacks
    • Less potency
    • Required a high dose
    • Develops rapid resistance
    • Less penetration into tissues and fluids
    • Used only for Gram-negative bacteria

Chemistry and classification page 18

  • Formed by combining nalidixic acid, fluoride and a piperazine ring.
  • The fluoride ion was attached to overcome the drawbacks of the older quinolones.
  • The resulting broad-spectrum agents have
    • High potency
    • Less resistance development
    • More penetration into tissues and fluids
  • Classification as listed in the lecture overview
    • Generation I — Norfloxacin, Ofloxacin, Ciprofloxacin for enteric fever and typhoid fever.
    • Generation II — Levofloxacin for respiratory tract infection and typhoid fever, Lomefloxacin, Moxifloxacin which is most preferred by doctors.
    • Ofloxacin and levofloxacin differ as isomers.

Mechanism of action and resistance stated in the overview page 18

  • Fluoroquinolones inhibit
    • DNA gyrase in Gram-positive bacteria
    • Topoisomerase IV in Gram-negative bacteria
  • They have affinity for topoisomerase IV and the 2A1 subunit of DNA gyrase, which results in abnormality in the nicking and resealing of the bacterial DNA strand.
  • Because of the DNA abnormality, the cell releases exonucleases which lyse the cell.
  • Resistance — change in enzyme structure, change in enzyme affinity, and low penetration.

Uses and side effects from the overview page 18

Uses

  • Urinary tract infections, gonorrhea, gastroenteritis, typhoid fever
  • Bone, soft tissue and gynecological infections
  • Respiratory infections and tuberculosis
  • Gram-negative septicemia, meningitis and conjunctivitis

Side effects

  • GIT — nausea, vomiting, anorexia
  • CNS — dizziness, anxiety, headache, insomnia, tremors, seizures
  • Hypersensitivity — photosensitivity, swelling of lips, rashes
Do Not Confuse — Two Different Statements About the Same Enzymes The overview section lists DNA gyrase as the Gram-positive target and topoisomerase IV as the Gram-negative target.
The mechanism section on page 19 states the opposite assignment — DNA gyrase as the primary target in Gram-negatives and topoisomerase IV as the primary target in Gram-positives.
Both statements appear in this lecture. The detailed mechanism section is the one expanded below.

B. Fluoroquinolone Generations

The evolution runs from Gram-negative rods to respiratory cocci and finally to anaerobes.

Generations with spectrum and clinical application pages 18 to 19
Generation and agentsAntibacterial spectrum and focusClinical application
1st Generation

Figure 24. Summary of Fluoroquinolone Evolution. Lecturer's PPT · page 34
What to notice: four columns move left to right, and each column has the same three rows — agents, spectrum and key clinical uses. Reading the spectrum row across shows the pattern the lecturer wants — Gram-negative aerobic bacilli, then expanded Gram-negative including Pseudomonas plus atypicals, then enhanced respiratory pathogens including pneumococci, then anaerobes plus delafloxacin MRSA activity.

C. Mechanism of Action

Target 1 — DNA gyrase, topoisomerase II

  • Primary target in Gram-negative bacteria.
  • DNA gyrase introduces negative supercoils into double-stranded DNA to neutralise the positive supercoils created by replication forks.
  • Fluoroquinolones block this enzyme, halting DNA replication and blocking replication fork progression.

Target 2 — Topoisomerase IV

  • Primary target in Gram-positive bacteria.
  • Responsible for decatenation, mechanically separating the two linked circular daughter chromosomes after replication is complete.
  • Inhibition prevents cell division.

Why the effect is lethal rather than merely inhibitory page 19

  • Lethal double-strand breaks
    • Fluoroquinolones do not merely inhibit enzymatic activity.
    • They bind and freeze the enzyme-DNA complex mid-cleavage.
    • This traps DNA in a broken state, inducing lethal double-stranded genomic fragmentation.
  • Bactericidal dynamics
    • Because they destroy genomic integrity, fluoroquinolones are highly bactericidal.
    • Like aminoglycosides they exhibit concentration-dependent killing and a post-antibiotic effect.
  • A dual-targeting strategy
    • Because two separate essential replication enzymes are targeted, bacteria must simultaneously mutate both enzymes to achieve high-level resistance, which happens rarely.
Figure 25. Fluoroquinolone Mechanism of Action — DNA Gyrase and Topoisomerase IV Blockade. Lecturer's PPT · page 35
What to notice: the left column belongs to DNA gyrase — relieves positive supercoils ahead of the replication fork, and blockade stalls the fork. The right column belongs to topoisomerase IV — separates linked daughter chromosomes, and blockade prevents decatenation and cell division. The centre lock icon is the key concept, trapping the enzyme-DNA cleavable complex so that lethal double-strand breaks accumulate. The bottom band restates the dual-targeting strategy as a barrier to resistance.

D. Pharmacokinetics

Absorption and the cation chelation hazard page 19

  • Outstanding oral bioavailability
    • Ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin and moxifloxacin reach 70 to 95 percent oral bioavailability, allowing an easy IV to oral transition.
  • The cation chelation hazard
    • Oral absorption is severely compromised by multivalent metal cations, including antacids with magnesium or aluminium, calcium supplements, iron, sucralfate and dairy products.
  • Chelation mechanism
    • The quinolone carboxylic acid group chelates directly with metal ions — Mg2+, Al3+, Ca2+ and Fe2+.
    • This forms insoluble, non-absorbable complexes in the gut, completely blocking absorption and leading to therapeutic failure.
  • Wide tissue penetration
    • High therapeutic concentrations achieved in bone, lung, prostate and phagocytic cells.

Elimination and probenecid page 19

  • Active renal secretion
    • Most agents — ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, ofloxacin — are cleared primarily by the kidneys through glomerular filtration and active tubular secretion.
  • Probenecid blockade
    • Because tubular secretion is mediated by organic anion transporters, co-administration of probenecid blocks this active secretion and significantly raises serum fluoroquinolone levels.
  • Renal dose adjustments
    • Dosage reductions are mandatory when creatinine clearance is below 50 mL per minute, to prevent accumulation and CNS toxicity.
  • Moxifloxacin hepatic exception
    • Metabolised hepatically and excreted via the biliary system, so it requires no renal dose adjustment.
    • However it does not reach therapeutic urine levels, so it cannot be used to treat UTI.
Figure 26. Fluoroquinolone Pharmacokinetics — Bioavailability, Cation Chelation and Clearance. Lecturer's PPT · page 35
What to notice: panel 1 pairs the 70 to 95 percent oral bioavailability figure with the tissue icons — bone, lung, prostate and phagocytes. The chelation strip shows the insoluble complex forming with antacids, calcium, iron, sucralfate and dairy, and gives the practical rule — take the fluoroquinolone at least 2 hours before or 4 to 6 hours after those products. Panel 2 splits elimination into the renal route for cipro, levo and ofloxacin, including the probenecid interaction and the dose-adjust threshold at creatinine clearance below 50, against the hepatic and biliary route for moxifloxacin marked not for UTIs.

E. Resistance

Point mutations and affinity loss pages 19 to 20

  • Quinolone Resistance-Determining Region (QRDR)
    • Chromosomal point mutations map to specific, highly conserved amino acid segments of the target enzyme genes, known as the QRDR.
  • GyrA and ParC mutations
    • In Gram-negatives, point mutations occur in the gyrA gene, encoding the A subunit of DNA gyrase.
    • In Gram-positives, mutations map to the parC gene, encoding topoisomerase IV.
  • Severe binding deficits
    • A single amino acid substitution in the QRDR alters the antibiotic-binding pocket and reduces binding affinity 10 to 100-fold, allowing replication to proceed despite the drug.
  • Rapid gonococci escape
    • Due to widespread empirical use, Neisseria gonorrhoeae developed rapid gyrA point mutations, so fluoroquinolones are no longer recommended for gonorrhea.
    • In the 1990s ciprofloxacin was first-line for gonorrhea, but high exposure allowed a single gyrA point mutation to arise and spread globally.
    • Ceftriaxone is now the standard of care for gonorrhea.

Efflux pumps and porin mutations page 20

  • Multidrug active efflux pumps
    • Pathogens including Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae and Mycobacterium tuberculosis express transmembrane pumps that actively extrude the drug from the cytoplasm.
  • Gram-negative porin loss
    • In Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Serratia, mutations delete or down-regulate outer membrane porins such as OprD, preventing the hydrophilic drug from crossing the outer membrane.
  • Rapid resistance spread
    • Plasmid-mediated resistance genes, for example Qnr proteins that protect DNA gyrase, are now common and lead to rapid multidrug cross-resistance.
  • Reminder from the lecture: resistance can accumulate. A single bacterial isolate can carry more than one mechanism, producing progressively higher resistance.
Figure 27. Fluoroquinolone Resistance — QRDR Mutations, Efflux Pumps and Porin Loss. Lecturer's PPT · page 35
What to notice: panel 1 shows the QRDR mutation converting strong binding into 10 to 100-fold lower drug binding, with the gonorrhea note attached. Panel 2 shows active extrusion by efflux pumps in S. aureus, S. pneumoniae and M. tuberculosis. Panel 3 shows porin loss or down-regulation, specifically OprD, in Pseudomonas and Serratia, plus the plasmid qnr protein shielding DNA gyrase.

F. Toxicity

Must Know — What Restricts This Class Cartilage damage.
Tendon rupture.
QTc prolongation.
Dysglycemias.

FDA warnings and connective tissue risks page 20

  • Tendinitis and tendon rupture
    • Can cause bilateral Achilles tendon rupture or tendinitis, particularly the Achilles tendon.
    • The mechanism is chelation of magnesium, which disrupts collagen synthesis and extracellular matrix integrity.
    • High risk in the elderly, in renal failure, or with concurrent corticosteroid use.
  • Cartilage damage or arthropathy
    • Because they damage growing weight-bearing articular cartilage, fluoroquinolones are strictly contraindicated in children under 18 and in pregnancy, unless no alternatives exist such as in anthrax or cystic fibrosis.
  • Aortic aneurysm and dissection
    • The FDA warns that fluoroquinolones can double the risk of aortic aneurysm rupture or dissection, because collagen disruption extends to the vascular wall. Avoid in high-risk cardiovascular patients.

Cardiac and systemic toxicities page 20

  • QTc interval prolongation
    • Newer respiratory agents, levofloxacin and moxifloxacin, block cardiac IKr potassium channels and prolong the ventricular action potential.
    • Absolutely contraindicated with class IA or class III antiarrhythmics such as amiodarone and sotalol.
  • Central nervous system toxicity
    • Quinolones inhibit GABA binding to its receptors, presenting as headache, dizziness, insomnia and occasionally severe seizures. Avoid in patients with pre-existing CNS lesions.
  • Dysglycemias
    • Gatifloxacin was withdrawn from clinical use because of severe hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia.
    • Current agents still carry warnings for glucose fluctuations in diabetic patients.
  • Phototoxicity
    • Exposure to UVA light can trigger painful phototoxic skin reactions with sunburn-like blistering. Patients should avoid direct sunlight during therapy.
  • Practical rule: recognise adverse effects early and discontinue the drug when necessary, rather than continuing treatment through a potentially serious toxicity.
Figure 28. Fluoroquinolone Toxicity — Tendons, Cartilage, QTc, CNS and Glucose. Lecturer's PPT · page 36
What to notice: the left FDA column stacks the three connective tissue risks — tendinitis and Achilles rupture with the risk-amplifier list of elderly, renal failure and corticosteroids, cartilage arthropathy with the under-18 and pregnancy contraindication, and aortic aneurysm and dissection. The right column holds the systemic risks — QTc prolongation leading to torsades with the antiarrhythmic avoid-list, CNS toxicity from GABA inhibition, dysglycemia, and phototoxicity from UVA.
