H. Clinical Outlook and the Restraint Mandate

  • Fluoroquinolones represent one of the most potent broad-spectrum oral classes.
    • However, historical overuse led to rising resistance among common enterobacteria.
    • This has compromised the clinical power of the class.
  • The FDA has issued safety alerts emphasising serious side effects.
    • Achilles tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy and aortic dissection frequently outweigh the benefit for minor infections such as bronchitis, sinusitis or uncomplicated UTI.
  • The clinical consensus is restraint.
    • Do not prescribe when a narrower agent such as amoxicillin or nitrofurantoin will work.
  • Reserve them for severe, systemic or hospital-acquired infections such as osteomyelitis, hospital pneumonia or Pseudomonas bacteremia.

The restraint mandate page 20

  • Restricting quinolone use
    • Because of rising global resistance and serious safety concerns, major guidelines restrict fluoroquinolones to cases where no safe alternative exists.
  • Preservation for severe niches
    • Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia
    • Complicated osteomyelitis
    • Nosocomial pneumonia
    • Multi-drug resistant tuberculosis
  • Avoiding collateral damage
    • Empirical use for simple self-limiting bronchitis or uncomplicated lower UTI is actively discouraged in modern stewardship programs.

Stewardship action roadmap pages 20 to 21

  • De-escalation protocols
    • Start with narrow-spectrum agents such as nitrofurantoin for simple cystitis to bypass empirical fluoroquinolone exposure, then de-escalate once susceptibilities are known.
  • Patient risk stratification — screen before choosing
    • Advanced age above 60
    • Chronic kidney disease
    • Corticosteroid use
    • G6PD status
    • Pre-existing QTc prolongation
  • Rigorous monitoring
    • Watch for early toxicity signals — Achilles tendon pain, severe sunlight sensitivity or skin irritation.
    • Promptly discontinue therapy if they appear.

Tab Summary

Fluoroquinolones condensed

  • Mechanism
    • Inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV.
    • Trap the enzyme-DNA cleavable complex, producing lethal double-strand breaks.
    • Dual targeting means high-level resistance needs two mutations.
  • Choosing between the three systemic agents
    • Ciprofloxacin — best classic Pseudomonas, weaker pneumococcus.
    • Levofloxacin — respiratory plus Pseudomonas, renally cleared.
    • Moxifloxacin — anaerobes, hepatic and biliary clearance, never for UTI.
  • Kinetics
    • 70 to 95 percent oral bioavailability supports an easy IV to oral switch.
    • Chelation by magnesium, aluminium, calcium, iron, sucralfate and dairy causes treatment failure.
    • Probenecid blocks tubular secretion and raises levels.
  • Resistance
    • QRDR point mutations in gyrA and parC, worth a 10 to 100-fold binding loss.
    • Efflux pumps, OprD porin loss and plasmid qnr proteins.
    • Gonorrhea now goes to ceftriaxone because of exactly this.
  • The safety profile that now restricts the class
    • Tendinitis and Achilles rupture, cartilage arthropathy and aortic dissection
    • QTc prolongation, CNS effects from GABA inhibition and dysglycemia
    • UVA phototoxicity and C. difficile

XIII — Common and Serious Adverse Effects of Antibiotics

Four buckets of harm — immune reactions, organ toxicity, superinfection and interactions — plus the populations where drug choice narrows sharply.

A. Hypersensitivity Reactions and Their Management

The nature of the reaction page 21

  • Classified as a Type A or unpredictable reaction.
  • These are immune-mediated responses, ranging from mild skin rashes to severe anaphylaxis.
  • They can be IgE-mediated or non-IgE mediated.

The four classic types

  • Type I — IgE-mediated and immediate, presenting as urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm and anaphylaxis.
  • Type II — antibody-mediated cytotoxic reactions against cell surfaces, for example hemolytic anemia.
  • Type III — immune complex deposition, for example serum sickness and vasculitis.
  • Type IV — T-cell mediated and delayed, for example contact dermatitis and severe cutaneous reactions.
Figure 31. Types of Hypersensitivity — Immune Mediated Reactions. Lecturer's PPT · page 21
What to notice: the four panels are ordered I to IV, and each names the mediator first and the clinical picture second. Type I is the only IgE and immediate panel, which is why it is the one tied to anaphylaxis and to epinephrine. Types II and III are both antibody driven but differ by target — cell-bound antigen versus soluble immune complexes. Type IV is the only cell-mediated and delayed panel, so it appears days rather than minutes after exposure.

Effective management requires prompt recognition and a tailored approach to mitigate harm and ensure patient safety.

Table 10. Management of Antibiotic Hypersensitivity Reaction page 21
ManagementDescription
Immediate discontinuation Promptly stop the suspected antibiotic.
For severe reactions such as anaphylaxis, stabilise the patient's airway, breathing and circulation.
Symptomatic relief Administer antihistamines for mild cutaneous symptoms.
Corticosteroids can reduce inflammation.
Epinephrine is crucial for anaphylaxis and is often combined with IV fluids or hydration to stabilise blood pressure.
Patient education and documentation Educate the patient about the specific antibiotic and the reaction type.
Ensure clear, visible and prominent documentation of the allergy in the medical record, to prevent medication error.
Alternatives and desensitization Identify safe alternative antibiotics.
Consider possible cross reactions with other drug classes.
In critical situations where the offending agent is irreplaceable, supervised desensitization or giving of controlled doses may be considered under specialist guidance.

B. Organ-Specific Toxicities

General principles page 21

  • Classified as a Type B or predictable reaction.
  • Involves direct damage to specific organs
    • Kidneys — nephrotoxicity
    • Liver — hepatotoxicity
    • Ears — ototoxicity
  • These are usually dose dependent.
  • Chemotherapeutic agents are more notorious for organ-specific toxicities.
  • When a serious adverse reaction appears, discontinue use, adjust the dosing or change the drug, and look for an alternative instead.
Figure 32. Organ-Specific Toxicities of High-Risk Antibiotics. Lecturer's PPT · page 21
What to notice: the figure is organised by organ, not by drug, so the same drug can appear in more than one panel. Trace aminoglycosides across the figure and they sit in the kidney panel as acute tubular necrosis and again in the ear panel, which is exactly the pairing the lecture stresses. The kidney panel carries the monitoring message, the liver panel carries the enzyme surveillance message, and the ear panel carries the irreversibility message.

Nephrotoxicity

Shared risk factors

  • Patient factors
    • Age above 65 years
    • Baseline chronic kidney disease with eGFR below 60
  • Physiologic state
    • Volume depletion, which concentrates the drug at the tubule
  • Treatment factors
    • Concurrent nephrotoxins such as NSAIDs and contrast
    • Prolonged therapy beyond 7 days

Drug patterns and monitoring

  • Aminoglycosides — acute tubular necrosis
  • Vancomycin — dose-related nephrotoxicity
  • Creatinine is used to measure nephrotoxic effects.
  • Drug level is constantly monitored
    • The trough, or the lowest level of the drug in the bloodstream, is the value monitored.
    • For vancomycin it is measured every 4th dose.
  • Elderly people have a poorer ability to eliminate the drug.
Must Know — Monitoring Changes Outcomes Therapeutic drug monitoring with individualized dosing reduces nephrotoxicity risk by 40 to 60 percent compared with empiric dosing.
This is the strongest single argument in the lecture for measuring levels rather than dosing by habit.

Hepatotoxicity

  • Drug-induced liver injury from antibiotics ranges from asymptomatic enzyme elevation to fulminant hepatic failure.
  • Class patterns
    • Macrolides — cholestatic hepatitis
    • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole — a mixed pattern of hepatocellular affection and cholestatic hepatitis
    • Anti-TB drugs, especially isoniazid and pyrazinamide, are notorious for causing hepatotoxicity
  • It is important to monitor liver enzymes in prolonged therapy.
    • Early recognition through systematic monitoring prevents progression to irreversible damage.

Ototoxicity

Which agent hits which structure

  • Cochlear toxicity
    • Amikacin
    • Tobramycin
  • Vestibular toxicity
    • Gentamicin
    • Causes vertigo and ataxia
  • Damage is often irreversible.
  • Higher risk in renal impairment.
  • Risk amplification — loop diuretics such as furosemide potentiate toxicity through synergistic hair cell damage.

Prevention and monitoring

  • Extended-interval dosing, meaning once daily, reduces toxicity versus divided dosing
    • Valid only when the drug is concentration dependent.
  • Baseline audiometry for therapy lasting more than 5 days
    • Weekly monitoring by an audiologist for prolonged courses.
  • Avoid concomitant ototoxins when possible.
  • Dose adjustment or complete stopping of the drug is mandatory in renal impairment.
  • Therapeutic drug monitoring to maintain peak below 10 mg per L
    • Especially for gentamicin and tobramycin.
Clinical Cue — Separating the Two Aminoglycoside Ear Injuries Hearing loss and tinnitus point to the cochlea, so think amikacin and tobramycin.
Vertigo and ataxia point to the vestibular apparatus, so think gentamicin.

Neurotoxicity

  • Antibiotics can induce toxicity to central and peripheral nervous systems.
    • Fluoroquinolones — seizures, confusion, psychosis, hallucinations and insomnia
    • Beta-lactams at high dose, specifically penicillin G, cefepime and imipenem — seizures, myoclonus and encephalopathy
  • Risk concentrates in patients with predisposing factors
    • Renal dysfunction
    • Advanced age
    • Underlying seizure disorders

Hematologic toxicity

  • Antibiotic-induced bone marrow toxicity ranges from mild cytopenias to life-threatening aplastic anemia.
    • Chloramphenicol — aplastic anemia
    • Linezolid — thrombocytopenia
    • Sulfonamides — hemolysis in G6PD deficiency
  • These require periodic CBC monitoring.

C. Superinfection

Definition page 21

  • Classified as a Type B or predictable reaction.
  • Due to prolonged antibiotic use, there is disruption of the body's normal microbiota.
  • Secondary infections then arise from opportunistic pathogens such as Clostridioides difficile and Candida species.

Risk factors

  • Drug-related exposure
    • Prolonged antibiotic courses beyond 7 days
    • Broad-spectrum antimicrobial agents
    • Prior antibiotic exposure within 90 days
  • Host vulnerability
    • Immunosuppression, for example chemotherapy and transplant recipients
    • Extremes of age, very young or elderly
  • Healthcare environment
    • ICU admission and critical illness
    • Indwelling devices such as catheters and central venous lines
Antibiotic-induced superinfection by organism type pages 21 to 22
SuperinfectionSignificance or manifestationsAgents most implicatedPrevention
Clostridioides difficile colitis The most clinically significant antibiotic superinfection. Fluoroquinolones
Clindamycin
Broad-spectrum beta-lactams		 Restrict high-risk agents.
Consider probiotics in select patients.
Fungal superinfection Oral and vaginal candidiasis.
Invasive candidiasis in the immunocompromised.		 Broad-spectrum antibiotics — fluoroquinolones, carbapenems and extended-spectrum penicillins Antifungal prophylaxis in high-risk patients.
Bacterial superinfection MRSA.
Vancomycin-resistant enterococci.
Multidrug-resistant Gram-negatives — ESBL producers and CRE.		 Any prolonged broad-spectrum exposure Antibiotic stewardship and timely de-escalation of therapy.

Special Populations

📌 Must Know — Pregnancy Safe options in all trimesters — penicillins and most cephalosporins.
Avoid throughout pregnancy — tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides.
Pregnancy avoid-list with the reason attached page 22
Class to avoidReason given in the lecture
TetracyclinesPermanent tooth discoloration.
Bone growth inhibition.
FluoroquinolonesCartilage toxicity, based on animal data.
AminoglycosidesFetal ototoxicity, except when needed for severe infections.
Pediatric age-specific contraindications page 22
Drug and age cutoffReason
Tetracyclines — under 8 yearsEnamel hypoplasia and permanent discoloration.
Fluoroquinolones — under 18 yearsArthropathy concerns.
Reserved for serious infections without alternatives.

Chloramphenicol — neonatesGray baby syndrome, a circulatory collapse from immature glucuronidation.

Exam Trap — The Two Numbers Look Alike Tetracyclines stop at under 8 years because the injury is to teeth.
Fluoroquinolones stop at under 18 years because the injury is to cartilage.
Mixing the two cutoffs is the most common error in this section.

D. Clinically Significant Drug-Drug Interactions

Figure 33. Clinically Significant Antibiotics Drug-Drug Interactions. Lecturer's PPT · page 22
What to notice: the entries group into three mechanisms rather than a random list — enzyme inhibition or induction affecting drug levels, additive toxicity where two agents hit the same organ, and chelation or absorption blockade in the gut. Reading it that way makes the pairs predictable instead of memorised one by one.

High-risk antibiotics page 22

  • High-risk antibiotics are agents with a high likelihood of causing severe, potentially life-threatening adverse effects or complications.
  • They should be used only when clearly indicated, with
    • Appropriate monitoring
    • Documentation
High-Yield Recap — Section Summary Antibiotics may cause dose-related toxicities, hypersensitivity reactions and superinfections.
Organ-specific toxicities vary by drug class and patient factors.
Clostridioides difficile infection is a major antibiotic-associated complication.
Careful antibiotic selection is required in special populations — pregnancy, pediatrics and the elderly.
Clinically significant drug-drug interactions can alter efficacy and safety.

E. Antimicrobial Resistance as an Adverse Outcome

  • Resistance can be considered either a predictable or an unpredictable reaction.
  • Development of bacterial resistance to antibiotics leads to
    • Treatment failure
    • Increased morbidity and mortality
Lecture-Specific Note This lecture places resistance inside the adverse-effects section, not only in the microbiology discussion.
The framing matters — resistance is treated as a harm caused by prescribing, which is what justifies the stewardship material in the later tabs.

Tab Summary

Antibiotic harm in four buckets

  • Hypersensitivity, the unpredictable Type A reaction
    • Types I to IV, from IgE anaphylaxis to delayed T-cell reactions.
    • Management order — stop the drug, support the ABCs, then antihistamine, corticosteroid or epinephrine.
    • Document the phenotype so the record helps rather than blocks future care.
  • Organ toxicity, the predictable Type B reaction
    • Kidney — aminoglycosides and vancomycin, monitored by creatinine and trough.
    • Ear — cochlear for amikacin and tobramycin, vestibular for gentamicin.
    • Liver — macrolides, TMP-SMX, isoniazid and pyrazinamide.
    • Nervous system — fluoroquinolones and high-dose beta-lactams.
    • Marrow — chloramphenicol, linezolid and sulfonamides.
  • Superinfection
    • C. difficile colitis is the most clinically significant one.
    • Highest-risk agents are fluoroquinolones, clindamycin and broad-spectrum beta-lactams.
    • Fungal and resistant bacterial superinfection follow the same exposure logic.
  • Interactions and special populations
    • Interaction risk clusters as enzyme effects, additive toxicity and chelation.
    • Pregnancy — penicillins and most cephalosporins are safe, and tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides are avoided.
    • Pediatrics — tetracyclines under 8, fluoroquinolones under 18, sulfonamides and chloramphenicol in neonates.

XIV.01 to 02 — Core Vocabulary and Rational Antibacterial Therapy

The comprehensive reviewer opens by fixing the language, then gives a seven-step prescribing framework built around host, organism and drug.

01 — Rapid Review: The Big Picture

Table 11. Core Vocabulary page 22
TermMeaningPractical significance
Antimicrobial Natural or synthetic agent that kills or inhibits microorganisms. Includes antibacterial, antiviral, antifungal and antiparasitic drugs.
Antibiotic Traditionally a microbial product that inhibits another microorganism.
Commonly used to mean antibacterial drugs.		 Usage often overlaps with antibacterial.
Bactericidal Causes irreversible bacterial death. Often preferred in endocarditis, meningitis, severe infection or marked immunosuppression.
Context matters.
Bacteriostatic Reversibly inhibits growth and relies more on host clearance. Not intrinsically weaker.
Clinical efficacy depends on organism, site, exposure and host.
Selective toxicity Greater injury to the microorganism than to the host. Achieved by targeting the cell wall, the 70S ribosome, folate synthesis or bacterial enzymes.
Spectrum Range of susceptible organisms. Broad empiric coverage should be narrowed once data permits.
Superinfection New infection during therapy, often from microbiome disruption or resistant organisms. Think C. difficile, Candida or resistant Gram-negative organisms.
Post-antibiotic effect Persistent suppression after drug concentration falls below the MIC. Supports extended intervals for aminoglycosides and other concentration-driven agents.

02 — Rational Antibacterial Therapy

Table 13. A structured prescribing framework pages 22 to 23
StepWhat to assessCommon pitfall
1. Diagnose Syndrome, infection site, severity, need for source control, and colonization versus infection. Treating noninfectious inflammation or treating colonization.
2. Sample Obtain appropriate cultures before antibiotics, when this will not dangerously delay therapy. Poor sample quality, or cultures drawn after several doses.
3. Predict Likely organisms based on site, host, exposure, healthcare contact and the local antibiogram. Using a memorized spectrum without local ecology.
4. Select Efficacy, safety, suitability, penetration, interactions, cost and guideline fit. Equating broader coverage with better care.
5. Dose PK/PD target, renal and hepatic function, body size, critical illness and extracorporeal support. Standard dosing despite altered clearance or volume.
6. Reassess Clinical response, cultures, biomarkers, toxicity, route and source control at 48 to 72 hours. Continuing unnecessary combination or IV therapy.
7. Complete Shortest effective duration.
Document the indication and a stop or review date.		 Prolonging therapy just to be safe.

Empiric, definitive and prophylactic therapy

The three prescribing intents page 23

  • Empiric therapy
    • Begins before organism confirmation, based on syndrome, severity, risk factors and local resistance.
  • Definitive therapy
    • Culture-directed. Narrow the spectrum, optimise dose and duration, and remove redundant agents.
  • Chemoprophylaxis
    • Prevents a defined infection in a defined risk window. Timing and limited duration are essential.

Source control page 23

  • Drain abscesses
  • Remove infected devices
  • Debride necrotic tissue
  • Relieve obstruction
Must Know Drugs alone may fail.
Without source control, an otherwise correct antibiotic choice can still lose.
Key Differentiator — Empiric versus Definitive Empiric asks what the organism is likely to be, so it is driven by epidemiology and severity.
Definitive asks what the organism is, so it is driven by the culture and susceptibility result.
The transition between the two is the 48 to 72 hour antibiotic timeout.

Tab Summary

Core concepts and the prescribing framework

  • Vocabulary that changes decisions
    • Bactericidal versus bacteriostatic matters most in endocarditis, meningitis and immunosuppression.
    • Selective toxicity is achieved through wall, ribosome, folate and enzyme targets.
    • Post-antibiotic effect is what justifies extended dosing intervals.
  • Seven prescribing steps
    • Diagnose, Sample, Predict — establish that infection exists and what is likely causing it.
    • Select and Dose — match spectrum, penetration and PK/PD to the patient.
    • Reassess and Complete — the 48 to 72 hour timeout and the shortest effective course.
  • Three factor sets to weigh
    • Host — immunity, organ function, allergy phenotype, devices, site.
    • Organism — identity, burden, enzymes, porins, efflux, biofilm.
    • Drug — spectrum, penetration, PK/PD index, toxicity and interactions.
  • Three prescribing intents
    • Empiric before the organism is known.
    • Definitive once the culture returns.
    • Prophylactic within a defined risk window.
  • One non-drug rule
    • Source control comes first, because drugs alone may fail.

XIV.03 to 04 — Susceptibility Testing, PK/PD, Resistance and Stewardship

How the laboratory number is generated, what exposure pattern each class needs, and how resistance is acquired and contained.

03 — Susceptibility Testing, MIC and MBC

Table 15. MIC and MBC page 23
MeasureDefinitionInterpretation
MIC Lowest antimicrobial concentration preventing visible growth after standardized incubation. Compared with organism and drug breakpoints to classify susceptible, intermediate or resistant.
MIC is not a universal potency ranking across drugs.
MBC Lowest concentration that kills approximately 99.9 percent of the starting inoculum. Determined by subculture from non-growing tubes or wells.
The MBC to MIC ratio may suggest tolerance but is not routinely required.
Breakpoint Threshold integrating MIC distributions, PK/PD, dosing and clinical outcome data. Specific to the species, drug, method and standards body.
Can change over time.
Zone diameter Inhibition zone in disk diffusion. Translated by standardized tables.
Not simply interchangeable with MIC.
📌 Must Know — Important Correction About MIC A lower MIC does not automatically mean one antibiotic is clinically superior to another.
Compare the MIC with that drug's own breakpoint, the achievable exposure, the infection site and the dosing regimen.
Table 16. Common laboratory methods page 23
MethodPrincipleStrength and limitation
Broth dilutionSerial concentrations in broth.
The lowest clear well is the MIC.		Reference quantitative method.
Labor-intensive when done manually.
Agar dilutionDrug concentrations incorporated into the agar.Good for many isolates at once.
Technically demanding.
Gradient diffusion, E-testA gradient strip intersects the inhibition ellipse at the MIC.Convenient quantitative estimate.
Method-specific limitations.
Disk diffusionZone around a fixed-content disk.Simple and inexpensive.
Categorical rather than a direct MIC.
Automated systemsInstrumented growth detection and interpretation.Fast workflow.
Unusual resistance may require confirmation.
Table 17. PK/PD patterns page 23
Pattern and indexTypical classesDosing implication
Time-dependent
percent fT above MIC		 Beta-lactams Maintain free concentration above the MIC.
Shorter intervals or prolonged or continuous infusion may improve target attainment in selected severe infections.
Concentration-dependent
Cmax to MIC		 Aminoglycosides A higher peak relative to the MIC improves killing.

Exposure-dependent
fAUC to MIC		 Vancomycin
Fluoroquinolones

Tetracyclines		 Optimise total exposure over 24 hours while respecting toxicity.

Key Differentiator — Three Questions, Three Indices Beta-lactams ask how long the drug stays above the MIC.
Aminoglycosides ask how high the peak climbs above the MIC.
Vancomycin and fluoroquinolones ask how much total exposure accumulates over a day.

Synergy, antagonism and combination therapy

When combinations help page 23

  • Synergy — the combined effect exceeds the expected additive effect
    • Beta-lactam plus aminoglycoside in selected enterococcal infections
    • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole sequential folate blockade
  • Combination indications
    • Broaden urgent empiric coverage
    • Treat polymicrobial infection
    • Obtain synergy
    • Prevent resistance in high-burden infections
    • Treat diseases requiring multidrug regimens, for example tuberculosis

What combinations cost page 23

  • Harm to the patient
    • Additive toxicity
    • Drug interactions
    • C. difficile risk
  • Harm to the ecosystem
    • Selection pressure favouring resistant organisms
  • Harm to the regimen itself
    • Possible antagonism between the two agents
    • Expense without added benefit
Must Know De-escalate promptly when cultures and clinical trajectory permit.

04 — Antimicrobial Resistance and Stewardship

Table 18. Resistance mechanisms page 23
MechanismExampleResponse
Drug destruction or modification Beta-lactamases.
Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes.
Chloramphenicol acetyltransferase.		 Use a stable agent or a validated inhibitor combination when appropriate.
Altered target mecA and PBP2a in MRSA.
Altered PBPs in pneumococcus.
Ribosomal methylation.
gyrA and parC changes.		 Select a different active class.
Avoid relying on an affected target.
Reduced permeability Gram-negative porin loss. Can combine with efflux and enzymes to cause high-level resistance.
Efflux Tetracycline, macrolide and fluoroquinolone pumps. Raises the intracellular exposure requirement.
Cross-resistance may occur.
Pathway bypass or overproduction Altered folate enzymes or excess PABA. Weakens antimetabolite action.
Biofilm and persisters Devices, prostheses and chronic airway infection. Source control and prolonged or targeted regimens may be needed.

Genetic routes page 23

  • Spontaneous mutation followed by selection under antimicrobial pressure.
  • Horizontal gene transfer
    • Conjugation through plasmids
    • Transformation from free DNA
    • Transduction by bacteriophages
  • Mobile elements such as transposons and integrons can cluster multiple resistance genes together.

Why clustering matters

  • Because integrons and transposons package several genes as one unit, a single transfer event can deliver multidrug resistance at once.
  • This is why exposure to one agent can select for organisms resistant to several.
  • It is also why de-escalation is framed as a resistance-control measure, not only a cost measure.

Stewardship checklist — the eight rights page 23

  • Before starting
    • Right indication — document suspected or confirmed infection.
    • Right sampling — cultures before therapy if safe.
  • Choosing and giving the drug
    • Right drug — guideline-informed and antibiogram-informed.
    • Right dose — optimise PK/PD and adjust for organ dysfunction.
    • Right route — switch IV to oral when the patient is stable and the drug is absorbable.
  • Stopping and reviewing
    • Right duration — the shortest evidence-supported course.
    • Right review — an antibiotic timeout at 48 to 72 hours.
  • Beyond the prescription
    • Right prevention — vaccination, hand hygiene, isolation and device care.
High-Yield Recap MIC is interpreted against a breakpoint, never compared naively between drugs.
Beta-lactams are time-dependent, aminoglycosides are concentration-dependent, vancomycin and fluoroquinolones are exposure-dependent.
Resistance arises by six mechanisms and spreads by mutation plus horizontal transfer.
Stewardship is the eight rights, anchored by the 48 to 72 hour timeout.

Tab Summary

Testing, exposure and stewardship

  • What the laboratory number means
    • MIC is the lowest concentration preventing visible growth.
    • MBC kills 99.9 percent of the inoculum.
    • A lower MIC does not mean a better drug, because the breakpoint is drug-specific.
  • How the number is generated
    • Quantitative — broth dilution, agar dilution and the E-test.
    • Categorical — disk diffusion zone diameters.
    • Automated systems are fast but may need confirmation.
  • Three exposure patterns
    • Beta-lactams ask how long the level stays above the MIC.
    • Aminoglycosides ask how high the peak is.
    • Vancomycin and fluoroquinolones ask how much total exposure accrues in 24 hours.
  • Six resistance mechanisms
    • Drug destruction, altered target and reduced permeability
    • Efflux, pathway bypass and biofilm or persisters
  • How resistance travels
    • Spontaneous mutation under selection pressure.
    • Conjugation, transformation and transduction.
    • Transposons and integrons cluster several genes into one transferable package.
  • Stewardship
    • The eight rights, anchored by the 48 to 72 hour timeout.

XIV.05 — Cell-Wall and Cell-Membrane Agents

The reviewer restates every cell-wall class in one fixed format — mechanism, effect, spectrum, uses, kinetics, adverse effects, resistance and exam pearls.

Class anchor page 23

  • Beta-lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins, inhibit transpeptidation and weaken peptidoglycan.
    • They kill actively dividing bacteria.
    • Major resistance pathways are beta-lactamase production, altered PBPs, reduced porin entry and efflux.
Table 19. Penicillins pages 23 to 24
DomainHigh-yield review
MechanismThe beta-lactam ring acylates PBPs and blocks peptidoglycan cross-linking.
EffectBactericidal.
Time-dependent.
SpectrumNatural — streptococci, susceptible meningococci, spirochetes.
Anti-staphylococcal — MSSA.
Aminopenicillins — add enterococci and selected Gram-negatives.
Antipseudomonal — broader Gram-negative activity.
Clinical usesPenicillin G or V for susceptible streptococci and syphilis.

Amoxicillin or ampicillin for susceptible respiratory and enterococcal pathogens.
Piperacillin-tazobactam for broad severe polymicrobial and Gram-negative coverage.

Probenecid reduces tubular secretion.
Penicillin G is acid-labile.
Penicillin V and amoxicillin are the oral options.

Seizures at high levels.
Aminopenicillin rash is common with EBV.

Inhibitors protect only against susceptible enzymes.
📌 Exam and clinical pearlsDo not label every rash as anaphylaxis.
Clarify timing, symptoms and severity, since allergy delabeling improves care.
Anti-staphylococcal penicillins cover MSSA and not MRSA.
Table 20. Beta-lactamase inhibitors page 24
GroupPartners and key point
Clavulanate, sulbactam, tazobactamSuicide inhibitors of many class A beta-lactamases.

If the organism is resistant because of an altered PBP, porin loss or an efflux pump, the combination gains nothing.

DomainHigh-yield review

Cephalosporins — ceftazidime and cefepime for Pseudomonas, ceftaroline for MRSA, ceftriaxone for neither.
Carbapenems — broadest coverage, meropenem for CNS, ertapenem is not antipseudomonal, imipenem seizes.

Daptomycin — never for pneumonia, and monitor CPK.

Tab Summary

Cell-wall and membrane review in one pass

  • Shared mechanism
    • All beta-lactams bind PBPs, block transpeptidation and are time-dependent.
    • All are defeated by the same four routes — enzymes, altered PBPs, porin loss and efflux.
  • The exception list that carries the marks
    • Anti-staphylococcal penicillins — MSSA only.
    • Ceftazidime and cefepime — Pseudomonas.
    • Ceftaroline — MRSA.
    • Ertapenem — not antipseudomonal.
    • Meropenem — the CNS carbapenem.
  • Inhibitor logic
    • An inhibitor helps only against an enzyme it can block.
    • Vaborbactam plus meropenem is the KPC-directed pairing.
  • Glycopeptide and membrane rules
    • Vancomycin loses to a beta-lactam for MSSA.
    • Oral vancomycin does not treat systemic infection.
    • Daptomycin is never used for pneumonia, and CPK is monitored.

XIV.06 — Protein Synthesis Inhibitors

Six tables in the same eight-row format, covering every ribosomal agent from aminoglycosides through the oxazolidinones.

Ribosomal selectivity anchor page 24

  • Bacterial ribosomes are 70S, built from a 30S and a 50S subunit.
  • Mammalian cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, which is what creates the therapeutic window.
  • Mitochondrial ribosomes resemble bacterial machinery, which helps explain selected class toxicities.

An erm gene that methylates that region can be inducible, so the plate reads clindamycin-susceptible while the organism can switch resistance on during therapy.
The D-shaped blunting of the clindamycin zone next to the erythromycin disk is what reveals it.

Tetracyclines — 30S A-site, static, blocked by cations, doxycycline is the rickettsial exception.
Macrolides — 23S translocation, QT and CYP3A4, azithromycin is the low-interaction member.
Clindamycin — 50S, toxin suppression, C. difficile, D-test.
Chloramphenicol — peptidyl transferase, two distinct marrow toxicities.
Linezolid — blocks initiation complex formation, covers MRSA pneumonia, watch platelets and serotonin.

Tab Summary

Protein synthesis review in one pass

  • Read each table by its last row
    • The exam pearls row is where the lecturer places the distinguishing fact.
  • The six pearls, compressed
    • Aminoglycosides — no anaerobes, because uptake needs oxygen.
    • Tetracyclines — separate from cations, stay upright, and doxycycline is the rickettsial exception.
    • Macrolides — check QT and interactions, and azithromycin is not reliable monotherapy where pneumococcal resistance is high.
    • Clindamycin — ask for the D-test.
    • Chloramphenicol — two different marrow toxicities.
    • Linezolid — covers MRSA pneumonia where daptomycin cannot.
  • Effect patterns
    • Only aminoglycosides are reliably cidal in this block.
    • Linezolid is cidal against many streptococci but static against staphylococci and enterococci.

Tab Summary

Folate, DNA and the reviewer-only agents

  • TMP-SMX
    • Sequential folate blockade, often bactericidal in combination.
    • Drug of choice for PJP, Nocardia and Stenotrophomonas.
    • Monitor potassium, creatinine and CBC.
  • Fluoroquinolones
    • Trapped cleavable complexes cause double-strand breaks.
    • Among the respiratory agents, only levofloxacin is reliably antipseudomonal.
  • Three agents taught only here
    • Rifamycins — RNA polymerase, never monotherapy, orange secretions and heavy enzyme induction.
    • Metronidazole — reactive radicals, anaerobes below the diaphragm, metallic taste and neuropathy.
    • Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin — bladder only, never for pyelonephritis.
  • One artifact to recognise
    • Trimethoprim raises serum creatinine without lowering GFR, by blocking tubular secretion.

10 — Pregnancy, Lactation, Children and Older Adults

Pregnancy page 27

  • Use indication-specific, up-to-date references.
    • Beta-lactams and selected macrolides have extensive experience.
    • Avoid blanket statements, because gestational age, dose and indication matter.
  • 📌 Avoid tetracyclines routinely in pregnancy and during tooth development, when alternatives exist.
  • Avoid fluoroquinolones routinely when safer choices exist.
  • Aminoglycosides require a compelling indication and monitoring.
  • Sulfonamides require caution near term and in neonates.
    • Trimethoprim is a folate antagonist and needs a trimester-specific and indication-specific assessment.

Children and older adults page 27

  • Children
    • Dosing is weight-based and age-based.
    • Organ maturation changes clearance.
    • Doxycycline can still be appropriate for select rickettsial disease.
  • Older adults — selection is strongly influenced by
    • Renal function
    • Frailty
    • QT risk
    • Tendons
    • CNS effects
    • Polypharmacy
    • C. difficile risk

That conflicts with Table 21 and with Table 36 in the same reviewer, where ceftaroline is the MRSA cephalosporin and ceftriaxone is not.

Classic no-coverage reminders page 27

  • Gaps defined by oxygen requirement
    • Aminoglycosides — no anaerobes, because uptake needs oxygen.
    • Metronidazole — anaerobes and protozoa, and no aerobes.
  • Gaps defined by the Gram stain
    • Aztreonam — no Gram-positive organisms or anaerobes.
    • Vancomycin, daptomycin and linezolid — no Gram-negative organisms.
  • Gaps defined by Pseudomonas
    • Ertapenem — no reliable Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter or Enterococcus.
    • Ceftriaxone, ceftaroline and moxifloxacin — no reliable Pseudomonas.
  • Gaps defined by the infection site
    • Daptomycin — no pneumonia, since surfactant inactivates it.
    • Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin — not for pyelonephritis or bacteremia, since only urine levels are adequate.

Tab Summary

Spectrum, monitoring and the bedside checklist

  • Organism-first thinking
    • MSSA goes to an anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam, not vancomycin.
    • Enterococcus is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins.
    • Stenotrophomonas goes to TMP-SMX and resists carbapenems.
    • C. difficile needs oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin.
  • Harm recognised by pattern, not by drug name
    • IgE allergy, severe delayed immune reaction, predictable toxicity, microbiome injury and drug interaction.
    • Each pattern has its own immediate response.
  • Monitoring matched to class
    • Renal function and levels for vancomycin and aminoglycosides.
    • CBC for linezolid, chloramphenicol and sulfonamides.
    • ECG and electrolytes for macrolides and fluoroquinolones.
  • Life-stage rules
    • Pregnancy favours beta-lactams and selected macrolides.
    • Children are dosed by weight and age, with doxycycline retained for rickettsial disease.
    • Older adults concentrate every risk — renal decline, QT, tendons, CNS effects and C. difficile.
  • The closing checklist
    • Seven questions ending in one — what will trigger de-escalation.

1. The Whole Lesson in One Frame

Target map

  • CELL WALL — beta-lactams and vancomycin
    • Beta-lactams — penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, monobactams
    • Glycopeptides — vancomycin, teicoplanin, oritavancin
    • Others — bacitracin, fosfomycin, cycloserine

  • 50S RIBOSOME — macrolides, clindamycin, chloramphenicol, linezolid, streptogramins

  • DNA — fluoroquinolones
  • RNA — rifamycins

3. Cell Wall Agents

Penicillins

  • Mechanism — the beta-lactam ring acylates PBPs and blocks transpeptidation, so cross-linking fails.
    • The ring is a structural mimic of D-Ala-D-Ala, which is the molecular deception at the heart of the class.
    • Autolysins then degrade the weakened wall, so the cell lyses osmotically.
  • Effect — bactericidal and time-dependent, active only against dividing cells.
  • Families and the one line that matters for each
    • Natural — streptococci and syphilis, penicillin G is acid-labile.
    • Anti-staphylococcal — MSSA only, never MRSA.
    • Aminopenicillins — add enterococci, and rash with EBV.
    • Antipseudomonal — piperacillin-tazobactam for broad severe infection.
  • Four evasion strategies used against them
    • Beta-lactamase production
    • Altered PBPs
    • Reduced porin entry
    • Efflux
  • Toxicity — hypersensitivity, interstitial nephritis, diarrhea and C. difficile, cytopenias, seizures at high levels.
  • Kinetics — renal elimination, and probenecid blocks tubular secretion to raise levels.
📌 Must Know — Penicillin Pearls Do not label every rash as anaphylaxis. Clarify timing, symptoms and severity, since allergy delabeling improves care.
Anti-staphylococcal penicillins cover MSSA and not MRSA.

Cephalosporins

  • Generational trend — increasing Gram-negative coverage and decreasing Gram-positive coverage, until the fourth and fifth generations reverse part of that.
  • The exceptions that carry the marks
    • Ceftazidime and cefepime cover Pseudomonas.
    • Ceftaroline covers MRSA.
    • Ceftriaxone and cefotaxime penetrate the CSF.
    • Cephamycins add anaerobes.
  • Toxicities to name
    • Cefepime neurotoxicity in renal dysfunction
    • Ceftriaxone biliary sludging and the neonatal calcium concern
    • MTT side chain agents causing hypoprothrombinemia and a disulfiram-like reaction
  • Cross-allergy with penicillins is 5 to 10 percent.

Carbapenems, monobactams and inhibitors

  • Carbapenems bind multiple PBPs and resist many beta-lactamases.
    • Imipenem needs cilastatin to block renal dehydropeptidase, and carries the most seizure risk through GABA inhibition.
    • Meropenem is the CNS carbapenem.
    • Ertapenem is once daily and is not antipseudomonal.
  • Aztreonam is the monobactam
    • Covers aerobic Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas.
    • No Gram-positive and no anaerobic activity.
    • Safe in most beta-lactam allergy, except for the ceftazidime side-chain overlap.
  • Inhibitors
    • Clavulanate, sulbactam and tazobactam are suicide inhibitors of class A enzymes.
    • Avibactam and relebactam are non-beta-lactam inhibitors reaching class A, C and some D.
    • Vaborbactam plus meropenem targets KPC.
    • An inhibitor adds nothing when resistance is from altered PBP, permeability or efflux.

Glycopeptides and membrane agents

  • Vancomycin
    • Binds D-Ala-D-Ala with 5 hydrogen bonds and blocks transglycosylation and transpeptidation.
    • Gram-positive only, because the molecule is too large to cross the Gram-negative outer membrane.
    • Resistance — D-Ala-D-Lac in VRE with a 1000-fold affinity loss, and cell-wall thickening in VISA.
    • Red man syndrome is an infusion-rate reaction, not a true allergy, and slow infusion prevents it.
    • Oral vancomycin stays in the gut for C. difficile and treats nothing systemic.
  • Daptomycin
    • Depolarizes the Gram-positive membrane and is rapidly bactericidal.
    • Inactivated by pulmonary surfactant, so never for pneumonia.
    • Monitor CPK for myopathy, and watch for eosinophilic pneumonia.
  • Polymyxins bind LPS, are salvage therapy, and cause nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity.
  • Bacitracin blocks bactoprenol recycling and is topical.
  • Fosfomycin blocks MurA, and cycloserine blocks D-alanine racemase and ligase.

4. Protein Synthesis Inhibitors

Mini-table — one line per agent
AgentSite and stepThe line that gets asked
Aminoglycosides30S, irreversible, blocks initiation and causes misreadingNo anaerobes, because uptake is oxygen-dependent.
Tetracyclines30S, reversible, blocks the A siteChelated by cations.
Under 8 years is the cutoff.
Macrolides23S of 50S, blocks translocationQT prolongation and CYP3A4 inhibition, except azithromycin.
Clindamycin50S near the macrolide site, suppresses toxinStrongest C. difficile association.
D-test for inducible resistance.
Chloramphenicol50S peptidyl transferaseTwo marrow toxicities and gray baby syndrome.
Linezolid50S, blocks initiation complex formationCovers MRSA pneumonia where daptomycin cannot.

Details that separate close neighbours

  • Aminoglycoside individuality
    • Gentamicin — synergy workhorse, vestibular injury, vertigo and ataxia
    • Tobramycin — better against Pseudomonas, nebulized in cystic fibrosis, cochlear injury
    • Amikacin — resists many modifying enzymes, cochlear injury
    • Plazomicin — resistant Enterobacterales, trough-only monitoring
    • Spectinomycin — related agent, not a true aminoglycoside in use
  • Aminoglycoside escape enzymes — acetyltransferases, phosphotransferases and nucleotidyltransferases.
  • Neuromuscular blockade — reverse with calcium gluconate first, then neostigmine, and avoid the class in myasthenia gravis.
  • Tetracycline resistance genes — efflux, ribosomal protection and enzymatic inactivation, with tigecycline designed to evade the first two.
  • Macrolide resistance — erm methylation and mef efflux.
  • Linezolid safety — thrombocytopenia in about 30 percent beyond 2 weeks, plus MAO inhibition and serotonin toxicity risk.

5. Antifolates

  • The pathway
    • PABA becomes dihydropteroic acid through dihydropteroate synthase, then dihydrofolate, then tetrahydrofolate through dihydrofolate reductase, which feeds purine, pyrimidine and amino acid synthesis.
  • Where each drug cuts
    • Sulfonamides are PABA analogues that competitively inhibit dihydropteroate synthase.
    • Trimethoprim inhibits bacterial dihydrofolate reductase with 10,000 to 100,000-fold selectivity.
    • Pyrimethamine is the antiprotozoal counterpart.
  • Selective toxicity — bacteria must synthesise folate, while humans absorb preformed folate.
  • Sequential blockade at 5 to 1 converts two static drugs into an often bactericidal combination.
  • Niche indications — Pneumocystis jirovecii treatment and prophylaxis, Nocardia, Stenotrophomonas, CA-MRSA and UTI, but not reliable for group A streptococci.
  • Toxicity to recite
    • SJS and TEN
    • Crystalluria
    • G6PD hemolysis
    • Kernicterus near term and in neonates
    • Megaloblastic anemia, prevented by folinic acid or leucovorin
    • Hyperkalemia, since trimethoprim behaves like a potassium-sparing diuretic
    • Creatinine rise without a real fall in GFR
  • Resistance — altered enzymes, excess PABA, and reduced permeability or efflux.

6. Fluoroquinolones

  • Mechanism — inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, trap the cleavable complex, and cause lethal double-strand breaks.
    • The detailed section assigns gyrase as the Gram-negative primary target and topo IV as the Gram-positive primary target.
    • Dual targeting is why high-level resistance needs two mutations.
  • Agent selection
    • Ciprofloxacin — best classic Pseudomonas, weaker pneumococcus
    • Levofloxacin — respiratory plus Pseudomonas
    • Moxifloxacin — anaerobes, hepatic and biliary clearance, and never for UTI
  • Kinetics — 70 to 95 percent oral bioavailability, chelated by magnesium, aluminium, calcium, iron, sucralfate and dairy, and probenecid raises levels.
  • Resistance — QRDR point mutations in gyrA and parC, efflux, OprD porin loss and plasmid qnr proteins.
  • Toxicity
    • Tendinitis and Achilles rupture through magnesium chelation, worse in the elderly, in renal failure and with corticosteroids
    • Cartilage arthropathy, so under 18 years and pregnancy are contraindications
    • Aortic aneurysm and dissection
    • QTc prolongation through IKr blockade, avoid with amiodarone and sotalol
    • CNS toxicity through GABA inhibition, including seizures
    • Dysglycemia, the reason gatifloxacin was withdrawn
    • UVA phototoxicity
    • C. difficile and myasthenia gravis exacerbation

7. Agents Taught Only in the Reviewer

Mini-table — rifamycins, metronidazole and the urinary agents
AgentMechanismUseWarning
RifamycinsBind DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and block transcriptionMultidrug TB, meningococcal prophylaxis, prosthetic-device staphylococcal adjunct, rifaximin for gut indicationsNever monotherapy, since single-step rpoB mutations arise fast.
Orange-red fluids and enzyme induction.
MetronidazoleReduced to reactive radicals that damage DNAAnaerobes below the diaphragm, bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasisNo aerobic activity.
Metallic taste and neuropathy with prolonged use.
NitrofurantoinReduced to reactive intermediates hitting multiple targetsUncomplicated lower UTINot for pyelonephritis.

8. Testing, Exposure and Stewardship

  • MIC is the lowest concentration preventing visible growth, and MBC is the lowest killing 99.9 percent.
  • 📌 A lower MIC does not mean a better drug. Compare it with that drug's breakpoint, its achievable exposure, the infection site and the regimen.
  • Laboratory methods — broth dilution as reference, agar dilution, E-test gradient strip, disk diffusion which is categorical, and automated systems.
  • PK/PD indices
    • Beta-lactams — time above MIC, so prolong the infusion
    • Aminoglycosides — Cmax to MIC, so raise the peak and extend the interval
    • Vancomycin and fluoroquinolones — AUC to MIC, so optimise 24-hour exposure
  • Six resistance mechanisms — drug destruction, altered target, reduced permeability, efflux, pathway bypass, biofilm and persisters.
  • Genetic routes — spontaneous mutation with selection, plus horizontal transfer by conjugation, transformation and transduction, with transposons and integrons clustering genes.
  • Stewardship is eight rights — indication, sampling, drug, dose, route, duration, review and prevention.

9. Harm, Monitoring and Special Populations

Mini-table — organ, agent and the monitored value
OrganAgentsWhat is monitored
KidneyAminoglycosides, vancomycin, polymyxinsCreatinine and trough levels, vancomycin every 4th dose
CochleaAmikacin, tobramycinAudiometry beyond 5 days, peak below 10 mg per L
Vestibular systemGentamicinVertigo and ataxia on examination
LiverMacrolides, TMP-SMX, isoniazid and pyrazinamideLiver enzymes in prolonged therapy
Nervous systemFluoroquinolones, penicillin G, cefepime, imipenem, linezolid, metronidazoleNeurologic status, especially in renal dysfunction
MarrowChloramphenicol, linezolid, sulfonamidesPeriodic CBC, and weekly with prolonged linezolid
📌 Must Know — Pregnancy Safe in all trimesters — penicillins and most cephalosporins.
Avoid tetracyclines — tooth discoloration and bone growth inhibition.
Avoid fluoroquinolones — cartilage toxicity.
Avoid aminoglycosides — fetal ototoxicity, except for severe infection.
Caution with sulfonamides near term, since trimethoprim is a folate antagonist.
📌 Must Know — Pediatric Cutoffs Tetracyclines — under 8 years, because of enamel hypoplasia.
Fluoroquinolones — under 18 years, because of arthropathy.
Sulfonamides — neonates, because of kernicterus.
Chloramphenicol — neonates, because of gray baby syndrome.
Doxycycline remains appropriate for select rickettsial disease, which is the deliberate exception.

Hypersensitivity in four lines

  • Type I — IgE, immediate, anaphylaxis, treated with IM epinephrine.
  • Type II — antibody-mediated cytotoxicity, for example hemolytic anemia.
  • Type III — immune complexes, for example serum sickness.
  • Type IV — T-cell mediated and delayed.
  • Severe delayed reactions to name — SJS, TEN, DRESS, AGEP, immune hepatitis and interstitial nephritis.
  • Management order — stop the drug, support the airway, breathing and circulation, give antihistamine, corticosteroid or epinephrine as appropriate, then document the phenotype and plan alternatives or desensitization.

10. Classic No-Coverage Reminders

Aminoglycosides no anaerobes Aztreonam no Gram-positives Vancomycin, daptomycin, linezolid no Gram-negatives Daptomycin no pneumonia
Ertapenem no Pseudomonas Ceftriaxone, ceftaroline, moxifloxacin no Pseudomonas Nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin no pyelonephritis Metronidazole no aerobes

11. If You See X, Think Y

Recognition table for stem clues
If the stem saysThink
Flushing and pruritus during a rapid infusionRed man syndrome from vancomycin, a rate-related reaction, not an allergy.
Bilateral Achilles pain in an elderly patient on steroidsFluoroquinolone tendinopathy.
Seizure in renal failure on a beta-lactamImipenem or cefepime or high-dose penicillin G neurotoxicity.
Vertigo and ataxia after an aminoglycosideGentamicin vestibular toxicity.
Hearing loss after an aminoglycosideAmikacin or tobramycin cochlear toxicity.
Watery diarrhea after clindamycinClostridioides difficile colitis, treated with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin.
Erythromycin-resistant and clindamycin-susceptible staphylococcusInducible resistance — ask for the D-test.
Falling platelets after two weeks of therapyLinezolid thrombocytopenia.
Delayed, irreversible pancytopenia after chloramphenicolIdiosyncratic aplastic anemia, distinct from the reversible dose-related suppression.
Newborn with circulatory collapse and gray discolorationGray baby syndrome from chloramphenicol.
Rising potassium and creatinine on an antibiotic for UTITrimethoprim, which spares potassium and blocks creatinine secretion.
Hemolysis after a sulfa drugG6PD deficiency.
Target lesions with mucosal involvement after a sulfa drugStevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Orange-red tears and urineRifampin.
Metallic taste with anaerobic coverageMetronidazole.
MRSA pneumonia needing an oral switchLinezolid, since daptomycin fails in the lung.
Treatment failure of an oral fluoroquinolone taken with antacidsCation chelation blocking absorption.
Inner ear infection in a patient whose livelihood depends on hearingChoose a class without ototoxicity, which is how the lecture frames the lincosamide option.

12. Final Sweep

High-Yield Recap — Last Look Before the Exam Selective toxicity exists because bacteria have a peptidoglycan wall, a 70S ribosome and a folate synthesis pathway that humans do not.
Cidal versus static is context-dependent, and the label alone does not predict outcome.
Every class has one structural exception that carries the marks — ertapenem, moxifloxacin, ceftaroline, daptomycin and oral vancomycin.
Monitoring is the treatment for the narrow-window drugs — vancomycin, aminoglycosides and linezolid.
Resistance is framed as an adverse effect of prescribing, which is why de-escalation at 48 to 72 hours is the single most repeated instruction in this lecture.

Tab Summary

How to use this cram sheet

  • Read it in three passes
    • Pass one — the target map and the mnemonics, to rebuild the skeleton.
    • Pass two — the value blocks, since numbers are the easiest marks to lose.
    • Pass three — the If You See X, Think Y table, which is closest to exam phrasing.
  • The five facts most likely to decide a question
    • Daptomycin is inactivated by surfactant, so never for pneumonia.
    • Oral vancomycin treats only the gut lumen.
    • Aminoglycosides cannot touch anaerobes, because uptake needs oxygen.
    • Moxifloxacin does not reach the urine.
    • Ceftaroline is the MRSA cephalosporin, and ceftazidime and cefepime are the antipseudomonal ones.
  • The three age cutoffs
    • Tetracyclines under 8 years.
    • Fluoroquinolones under 18 years.
    • Sulfonamides and chloramphenicol in neonates.
  • The one instruction repeated most often in this lecture
    • Reassess at 48 to 72 hours and de-escalate.
